claims.text: Begin by specifying the service the wall must deliver. Consider 100 m² of dry interior wall that must maintain a specified uniform color and at least 0.98 opacity continuously over the half-open interval [0, 10) years. Switching paints changes the coating schedule, material quantity, and upstream electricity demand. The identities, performance parameters, repainting schedules, inputs, emissions, substrate compatibility, electricity intensity range, and comparison tolerance for Paint A and Paint B are all pedagogical model assumptions. The inventory tracks fossil CO2 and fossil CH4, paired with published characterization factors. We first evaluate an intact smooth wall and then introduce a rough substrate.
claims.scope: Wall-coating pedagogical case: fixed service, activity, and emission assumptions paired with published characterization factors.

claims.text: Next, map material requirements across time. Paint A requires 0.05 kg/m² per coat and is assumed to last 5 years, requiring coats at year 0 and year 5; Paint B requires 0.06 kg/m² per coat and lasts 10 years. Over the full service window, Paint A therefore requires 100 m² × 0.05 kg/m²/coat × 2 coats = 10 kg, whereas Paint B requires 6 kg. Because the right endpoint at year 10 is excluded from [0, 10), no repainting is scheduled at year 10. The model also assumes zero application loss, instantaneous repainting with no downtime, no stripping of the prior coat before recoating Paint A, and constant product performance and manufacturing technology throughout the decade; these assumptions are what link each schedule to continuous service delivery.
claims.scope: Wall-coating pedagogical case: fixed service, activity, and emission assumptions paired with published characterization factors.

claims.text: Either Paint A or Paint B can fulfill the same functional service: maintaining the required color and opacity across 100 m² of wall for the specified decade. To compute the process model, that shared service must be translated into reference flows of 10 kg of Paint A or 6 kg of Paint B. As discussed in Functional Reference, the CML 2001 §2.3.4 paint example expresses the reference flow in terms of covered wall area and stores the required paint volume inside process data, whereas the International Reference Life Cycle Data System (ILCD) Handbook (2010, §6.4.1) permits either service-linked or product-oriented reference formulations depending on study purpose. Here we keep the wall service explicit and derive mass demands for processes scaled per kilogram of paint. Converting kilograms to grams merely rescales the same mass; deriving paint mass from wall service requires performance and repainting assumptions. Defining process data directly per kilogram avoids converting volume figures from the handbook and does not imply that arbitrary databases are interchangeable.
claims.scope: Wall-coating pedagogical case: fixed service, activity, and emission assumptions paired with published characterization factors.

claims.text: What happens if the comparison aligns purchased mass instead of delivered service? At an equal mass of 6 kg, Paint A—which must be applied twice over ten years—covers only 60 m², whereas Paint B covers the full 100 m². At a shared electricity intensity of θ = 0.1 kg CO2/kWh, supplying 6 kg yields 14.3802 kg CO2-eq for Paint A and 23.529 kg CO2-eq for Paint B, making Paint A appear lower. Once equal 100 m² ten-year service is restored, Paint A rises to 23.967 kg CO2-eq while Paint B stays at 23.529 kg CO2-eq, reversing the ranking in favor of Paint B. What changed first was the object of comparison: equal mass did not deliver equal wall area over ten years. Both outcomes belong strictly to this pedagogical model.
claims.scope: Wall-coating pedagogical case: fixed service, activity, and emission assumptions paired with published characterization factors.

claims.text: Before solving the process model, state what every row and column of the technology matrix represents. The four columns P-A, P-B, P-P, and P-E denote unit operations: supplying 1 kg of Paint A, supplying 1 kg of Paint B, preparing 1 m² of substrate, and supplying 1 kWh of electricity, respectively. The four rows carry units of kg A, kg B, m², and kWh. In matrix A, positive entries represent outputs and negative entries represent intermediate inputs consumed per unit operation, while vector s records the scaling factor (number of unit operations) for each process. For instance, the electricity entry in column P-B is -5 kWh/operation: the minus sign indicates electricity consumption during the production of 1 kg of Paint B, and its magnitude gives the electricity used per unit operation. Every matrix entry must be read in its row's physical unit rather than treated as a dimensionless number.
claims.scope: Wall-coating pedagogical case: fixed service, activity, and emission assumptions paired with published characterization factors.

claims.text: On a smooth substrate, no surface preparation is required. Placing the derived paint masses into their corresponding product rows gives the final demand vectors f_A = (10, 0, 0, 0)ᵀ and f_B = (0, 6, 0, 0)ᵀ in the row order defined above. The zero in the electricity coordinate means electricity is not delivered as a final external product; the electricity needed to manufacture paint is supplied internally between processes. How wall service maps into f_A and f_B is already fixed by coating performance, schedule, and substrate condition; solving the linear system simply scales the upstream activities needed to satisfy those demands.
claims.scope: Wall-coating pedagogical case: fixed service, activity, and emission assumptions paired with published characterization factors.

claims.text: Solving As = f row by row is straightforward. The first three rows fix the paint-supply and substrate-preparation scaling factors; in the fourth row, P-E must supply exactly enough electricity to offset intermediate electricity consumption across the first three columns. Paint A therefore activates 10 operations of P-A and 20 operations of P-E; Paint B activates 6 operations of P-B and 30 operations of P-E. For Paint B, the electricity balance reads (-5 kWh/operation × 6 operations) + (1 kWh/operation × 30 operations) = 0 kWh, while the Paint B row delivers 6 kg net. All generated electricity is consumed internally, leaving zero net external electricity demand. The calculation table records each step so s can be multiplied back into A to verify net delivery.
claims.scope: Wall-coating pedagogical case: fixed service, activity, and emission assumptions paired with published characterization factors.

claims.text: The equation As = f verifies that the modeled products and services meet the specified final demand. Because it does not list every chemical element or waste stream, it does not test full elemental mass conservation. The four processes here form an acyclic chain with no mutual feedback, which keeps the link from wall service to process demand transparent. By contrast, Process Networks uses mutually dependent processes with illustrative products and hypothetical emissions to show how recursive internal demand is solved. Those hypothetical emissions cannot be relabeled as CO2 or CH4 to borrow the characterization factors used here. Both examples verify balance strictly against their declared products and operations: one emphasizes translating service into demand, and the other emphasizes resolving process feedback.
claims.scope: Wall-coating pedagogical case: fixed service, activity, and emission assumptions paired with published characterization factors.

claims.text: Multiplying the activity vector by the intervention matrix yields the life cycle inventory: g = B(θ)s. Here θ denotes fossil CO2 emissions per kWh of electricity supply, whose uncertain range is examined below. At the display point θ = 0.3 kg CO2/kWh, Paint A generates 20 kg CO2 from paint production plus 6 kg from electricity, totaling 26 kg CO2, and 0.05 + 0.02 = 0.07 kg fossil CH4. Paint B totals 27 kg CO2 and 0.09 kg fossil CH4. Because each term equals emissions per unit operation times the number of operations, emissions sharing the same elementary flow identity sum directly.
claims.scope: Wall-coating pedagogical case: fixed service, activity, and emission assumptions paired with published characterization factors.

claims.text: The paint-supply and substrate-preparation columns record only non-electricity burdens; electricity generation burdens appear exclusively in column P-E, preventing double counting of power supply. The inventory tracks airborne fossil CO2 and fossil CH4 separately so that fossil CH4 matches the fossil-methane characterization factor applied next. Application equipment, labor, waste treatment, disposal, and recycling, other emissions, and other impact categories lie outside this pedagogical boundary. Within these declared boundaries, both gas totals are fully reproducible; the next step asks how to express their combined climate impact potential using a transparent metric.
claims.scope: Wall-coating pedagogical case: fixed service, activity, and emission assumptions paired with published characterization factors.

claims.text: 100-year Global Warming Potential (GWP-100) factors are taken from the October 7, 2025 errata replacement of IPCC AR6 WGI Table 7.15 using central values: 1 for CO2 and 28.1 for fossil CH4. Because the fossil-methane factor already incorporates the climate contribution from methane oxidation to CO2, no separate CO2 entry is added to the inventory for that oxidation pathway. Factor version, chemical species, and accounting convention jointly determine what the characterization step means.
claims.scope: Wall-coating pedagogical case: fixed service, activity, and emission assumptions paired with published characterization factors.
caveats: Citations retain the historical passage excerpts used when the case was authored alongside the corresponding sections of the primary report and errata table; the two records do not constitute independent scientific re-verification.
The selected factor version is not a universal default across all reporting frameworks, and the source table's factor uncertainty is not propagated in this single-parameter teaching model.

claims.text: Keeping units explicit makes characterization transparent: I = g_CO2 × (1 kg CO2-eq / kg CO2) + g_CH4 × (28.1 kg CO2-eq / kg fossil CH4). Canceling each gas mass unit leaves both terms in kg CO2-eq before summation. At the display point θ = 0.3, Paint A contributes 26 kg CO2-eq from CO2 and 1.967 kg CO2-eq from fossil CH4, totaling 27.967 kg CO2-eq; Paint B totals 29.529 kg CO2-eq. The denominator remains the entire ten-year, 100 m² wall service delivered by f. Expressing the result in kg CO2-eq records a relative metric score while the underlying inventory retains distinct physical gases—methane is not physically transformed into CO2.
claims.scope: Wall-coating pedagogical case: fixed service, activity, and emission assumptions paired with published characterization factors.

claims.text: Global Warming Potential (GWP) compares the time-integrated radiative forcing from an idealized unit-mass pulse emission of a greenhouse gas against an equal-mass reference pulse of CO2 over the same time horizon. The ratio itself is dimensionless; writing kg CO2-eq/kg gas documents which gas is converted on a CO2-equivalent basis. The resulting score I represents climate impact potential on that specific scale. Actual physical CO2 emissions must be read directly from the inventory, whereas local damages, temperature change at year 100, or endpoint damages require distinct physical models and evidence.
claims.scope: Wall-coating pedagogical case: fixed service, activity, and emission assumptions paired with published characterization factors.

claims.text: The ten-year wall service determines how many times Paint A must be applied, whereas the 100-year GWP horizon governs how each emission pulse is characterized. Assuming constant technology and grid intensity, this model aggregates activities over the decade and applies static pulse factors without tracking year-0 and year-5 emissions to a common calendar end date. Computing cumulative radiative forcing up to a fixed calendar year would require preserving emission timestamps and rebuilding the dynamic response model; simply dividing the static result by ten to report an annual average does not answer that dynamic question.
claims.scope: Wall-coating pedagogical case: fixed service, activity, and emission assumptions paired with published characterization factors.

claims.text: Next we examine how the comparison behaves as electricity emission intensity varies across its allowed domain. Let the grid CO2 intensity θ be fixed but unknown within [0.1, 0.5] kg CO2/kWh, with both Paint A and Paint B drawing from the same shared grid θ in every comparison. The quantity of interest is the paired difference Δ(θ) = I_B(θ) − I_A(θ) for delivering the complete service under identical substrate and electricity conditions; θ = 0.3 is merely a display point for inspecting the arithmetic. No probability distribution is assigned over [0.1, 0.5], nor does the interval arise from statistical sampling, so it is neither a confidence interval nor a representation of wall-to-wall variability. Characterization factors remain fixed at their central values, omitting the ±10.4 uncertainty reported for fossil CH4 in the source table. The calculation simply bounds Δ(θ) across all admissible values of the shared parameter θ.
claims.scope: Wall-coating pedagogical case: fixed service, activity, and emission assumptions paired with published characterization factors.

claims.text: Subtracting Paint A from Paint B under the same shared grid yields the affine expression Δ(θ) = -1.438 + 10θ kg CO2-eq per specified service on a smooth substrate. Because the slope is positive, the extrema occur at the domain endpoints, giving the exact paired difference interval [-0.438, 3.562] kg CO2-eq. The difference crosses zero at θ = 0.1438: Paint B is lower below the crossover, while Paint A is lower above it. Because the display point θ = 0.3 sits on only one side of the crossover, it cannot establish a strict global ranking across the full domain.
claims.scope: Wall-coating pedagogical case: fixed service, activity, and emission assumptions paired with published characterization factors.

claims.text: One can also compute each alternative's marginal range separately: [23.967, 31.967] kg CO2-eq for Paint A and [23.529, 35.529] kg CO2-eq for Paint B. Subtracting independent extremes (B's minimum minus A's maximum, and B's maximum minus A's minimum) yields [-8.438, 11.562] kg CO2-eq. While independent-extremes subtraction is a valid conservative outer envelope in interval arithmetic, here it breaks the shared-θ constraint by admitting impossible pairs in which one paint uses cleaner electricity while the other simultaneously uses dirtier electricity. Because the problem rules out such mismatched grids, the paired difference interval above tightens the bound substantially. Observing whether two marginal intervals overlap neither restores pairing nor tests any equivalence criterion.
claims.scope: Wall-coating pedagogical case: fixed service, activity, and emission assumptions paired with published characterization factors.

claims.text: Testing for a strict global ranking examines the sign of Δ(θ), whereas testing for equivalence within a tolerance examines its magnitude. This pedagogical case specifies a tolerance of ±4 kg CO2-eq per service and checks whether |Δ(θ)| ≤ 4 across all allowed θ. That threshold is constructed solely for illustration and must not be mistaken for a stakeholder-validated decision criterion. On a smooth substrate, the entire paired interval [-0.438, 3.562] lies inside ±4, satisfying the tolerance criterion everywhere even though no strict global ranking holds. These two findings answer separate questions—magnitude versus sign. Failing to rank two options does not by itself prove equivalence, no statistical equivalence test is performed here, and tightening the tolerance requires re-checking the interval against the new bound.
claims.scope: Wall-coating pedagogical case: fixed service, activity, and emission assumptions paired with published characterization factors.
caveats: The ±4 kg CO2-eq tolerance is constructed for pedagogical illustration and must not be treated as an independently validated empirical decision threshold.

claims.text: Now change only the initial substrate from smooth to rough while keeping the wall intact. Paint A still delivers the service directly, whereas Paint B requires preparing all 100 m² first. Wall area, service duration, paint mass, durability assumptions, process coefficients, shared θ, characterization factor versions, and comparison tolerance all remain unchanged. The third coordinate of Paint B's final demand increases from 0 to 100 m², activating 100 operations of P-P and raising electricity demand from 30 to 50 kWh. The substrate-preparation column was already present in matrix A; changing the demand vector is what activates it. Merely rescaling smooth-wall results per square meter does not conjure preparation activities into existence.
claims.scope: Wall-coating pedagogical case: fixed service, activity, and emission assumptions paired with published characterization factors.

claims.text: Recomputing along the same s → g → I pipeline at θ = 0.3 raises Paint B's inventory to 38 kg CO2 and 0.11 kg fossil CH4 and its climate score to 41.091 kg CO2-eq, while Paint A remains at 27.967 kg CO2-eq. The paired difference becomes Δ(θ) = 4.124 + 30θ, spanning [7.124, 19.124] kg CO2-eq across θ ∈ [0.1, 0.5]. Because this interval is strictly positive and lies wholly beyond +4, Paint A is strictly lower across the entire domain and the two options no longer satisfy equivalence within the tolerance under the rough-substrate model. This reversal has an explicit, traceable mechanism: Paint B triggers substrate preparation and additional electricity to deliver the same final service from a different starting condition. Even so, it remains a pedagogical model rather than a real-world procurement recommendation.
claims.scope: Wall-coating pedagogical case: fixed service, activity, and emission assumptions paired with published characterization factors.

claims.text: Consider three proposed recommendations: (1) "Paint A is lower at the display point, so choose Paint A for smooth walls too"; (2) "Reporting rough-wall results per square meter allows merging them with the smooth-wall case"; and (3) "Subtracting the independent extremes of the two marginal ranges is sufficient to judge the difference." For each claim, identify the unstated premise it requires, formulate the judgment actually supported by the model, and verify the rough-substrate electricity balance and gas inventories starting from Paint B's added preparation demand.
claims.scope: Wall-coating pedagogical case: fixed service, activity, and emission assumptions paired with published characterization factors.

claims.text: On a smooth substrate, the comparison must span the full admissible domain of shared θ: a single display point cannot establish a strict global ranking, whereas the full paired interval satisfies the ±4 kg CO2-eq tolerance criterion. On a rough substrate, Paint B's electricity balance reads (-5)×6 + (-0.2)×100 + 50 = 0 kWh, and column-by-column inventory summation must include both substrate preparation and the extra electricity. Rescaling outputs per square meter changes only the reporting unit; the initial substrates remain distinct, and the smooth-wall model still contains no preparation activity. Subtracting independent marginal extremes gives a conservative outer envelope, but knowing that both options share the same θ justifies using the tighter exact Δ(θ) interval. Tracing from service and coating quantities through f, s, g, and I makes every comparison condition auditable; real-world paint comparisons still require empirical performance, activity, emission, and decision criteria.
claims.scope: Wall-coating pedagogical case: fixed service, activity, and emission assumptions paired with published characterization factors.

claims.text: Placing the wall-coating case alongside international guidance reveals two shared baselines that transcend any specific material. First, comparisons are governed by decision context and symmetric system boundaries: the ILCD Handbook (2010) §5.3 assigns product comparisons and public comparative assertions to Situation A (micro-level decision support), excluding pure accounting studies (Situation C) from superiority procurement or policy claims; §§6.10.3–6.10.7 require equivalent boundaries and modeling rules, permitting omission only of strictly identical components while retaining partially correlated components for explicit correlation analysis alongside reasonable best/worst-case scenarios and uncertainty calculations. Second, uncertainty comparisons cannot fall back on isolated marginal intervals: the Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Protocol Product Standard (2011, §10.3.4) explicitly advises against comparing the marginal uncertainty ranges of Option A and Option B side by side, calling instead for evaluating parameter and scenario uncertainty on the comparison metric itself (such as A/B)—precisely the rationale for paired differencing under shared grid intensity above.
claims.scope: Cross-framework comparison of ILCD 2010 Situation A/C classification, boundary symmetry, and partial-correlation rules with GHG Protocol Product Standard (2011) §10.3.4 comparison-metric uncertainty guidance.
caveats: Boundary symmetry and paired evaluation eliminate methodological mismatch and shared-background noise, but do not substitute for verifying real-world use conditions, maintenance cycles, or unmodeled impact categories.

claims.text: Eliminating unpaired overlap does not mean running more random draws guarantees a valid statistical ranking. Building on the discussion of Monte Carlo sample size in Variability and Uncertainty, Heijungs (2020) draws two empirical samples of n = 16 each from the exact same parent distribution N(10, 1): a direct two-tailed t-test on the empirical samples gives p = 0.67—no evidence of a difference—yet feeding those noisy sample means with known standard deviations into a 100,000-run Monte Carlo simulation yields a spurious p ≈ 10⁻¹⁶. Increasing simulation runs shrinks only Monte Carlo standard error without correcting finite-sample bias in the inputs; simulation runs must therefore be bounded by the weakest empirical sample size (for example, at most 9 runs when input sample sizes are 16 and 9), and pedigree-matrix distributions lacking empirical sample counts cannot support large-sample significance tests. Using deterministic paired difference intervals and explicit tolerances in the wall case avoids masking input imprecision behind massive pseudo-sampling.
claims.scope: Connects Heijungs (2020) §§2.8–4 on Monte Carlo pseudo-significance with the deterministic paired-interval boundary used in the wall-coating case.
caveats: Deterministic paired sensitivity cleanly exposes shared-background cancellation and crossover thresholds, but multi-parameter comparisons with complex non-shared correlations still require joint uncertainty analysis backed by real empirical sample sizes.

claims.text: Even when arithmetic pairing and uncertainty checks hold, disclosing a product comparison to the public crosses an institutional "comparative assertion" threshold where major frameworks diverge substantively. Under ILCD 2010 (§5.2.5 and §§6.10.1–6.10.2, Provisions I and VI, pp. 34–35, 140–141, 145–146), three hard guardrails apply: first, any comparison disclosed beyond the commissioner and a named restricted audience—even a "non-assertive" side-by-side table or chart that omits explicit superiority wording—still triggers full comparative-assertion rules to prevent circumvention; second, comparative assertions disclosed to the public may never rely on life cycle inventory (LCI) results alone and must complete impact assessment and interpretation; third, §8.4 Provision III (pp. 283–284) strictly prohibits weighting in public comparative assertions because weights embed value choices. In addition, §§5.2.5 and 6.11 require pre-verified background and foreground datasets for comparative assertions, or else mandatory escalation from a single independent reviewer to an external review panel.
claims.scope: Documents ILCD 2010 §§5.2.5, 6.10.1–6.10.2, 6.11, and 8.4 rules on non-assertive anti-circumvention, prohibition of LCI-only assertions, weighting ban, and external review panel requirements.
caveats: Detailed review-scheme procedures reside in the companion ILCD document (Review schemes for LCA); this note verifies only the general admission thresholds in the main ILCD Handbook.

claims.text: In direct contrast to ILCD 2010's ban on weighting in public comparative assertions, European Commission Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279 on Product Environmental Footprint (PEF) adopts a regime of category-rule exclusivity paired with harmonized weighted scoring. Annex I §1 stipulates that product comparisons and comparative assertions are permitted only when conducted under a valid Product Environmental Footprint Category Rule (PEFCR); absent a valid PEFCR, studies are restricted to internal management or non-comparative external communication. Under a valid PEFCR, Annex I §5.2 and Annex II require global per-capita normalization and weighting across all 16 Environmental Footprint impact categories into a single overall score, anchoring Class C at the representative product benchmark (BM) and linearly interpolating Classes A through E using 0.30 and 0.85 factors between BM and sensitivity-derived theoretical best and worst scores. As the institutional counterweight for allowing weighted grading, Annex I §8 mandates independent third-party verification and validation aligned with EN ISO/IEC 17020:2012 for all external communications: any category shift exceeding 5% constitutes a material discrepancy, verifiers must hold at least 6 qualification points, and verification statements remain valid for at most 3 years.
claims.scope: Verifies PEFCR-gated comparisons, 16-category weighted single-score A–E performance classes, and mandatory third-party verification thresholds in Commission Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279 Annex I §§1, 1.1, 5.2.1–5.2.2, 8.1–8.5 and Annex II Table NN-9.
caveats: Commission Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279 is itself a non-binding recommendation; legally mandatory force arises only when incorporated into specific EU legislation such as the Batteries Regulation or Ecodesign delegated acts.

claims.text: A third boundary appears in single-indicator greenhouse gas accounting. The GHG Protocol Product Standard (2011) §§1.5, 5.3.2, 13.2, and Appendix A state clearly that, as written, the standard supports tracking a single product's carbon performance over time and assessing emission reductions, not making comparative assertions of overall environmental superiority against competing products. Any cross-product carbon comparison, label, or performance claim must additionally follow harmonized product rules that align the unit of analysis, system and temporal boundaries, and allocation methods, disclose data quality and uncertainty, and undergo third-party assurance. Every cross-framework clause in this section rests strictly on page-verified open-access primary sources (ILCD 2010, Commission Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279, GHG Protocol 2011, and Heijungs 2020); the book's uniform verification boundary for paywalled standards such as ISO 14044:2006 is documented in the Reading Guide.
claims.scope: Documents the GHG Protocol Product Standard (2011) §§1.5, 5.3.2, 13.2, and Appendix A boundary against comparative assertions and states the explicit verification boundary for paywalled ISO 14044:2006.
caveats: Clause-by-clause citation of the paywalled ISO 14044:2006 full text remains outside the open-source verification boundary until licensed primary text is held.

claims.text: Taken together, the wall-coating model and the three international frameworks demonstrate that a defensible product comparison requires two independent, non-substitutable qualifications. At the computational level, the analyst must fix a shared functional service, align system boundaries and shared background parameters—eliminating both unpaired overlap and Monte Carlo pseudo-significance exceeding empirical sample counts—and test ranking stability against tolerances and substrate changes. At the governance level, the analyst must distinguish internal improvement from category-rule benchmark grading (such as EU PEFCR Classes A–E) and public comparative assertions (where ILCD prohibits weighting and mandates external review panels, while the GHG Protocol Product Standard declines support as written). Any defensible comparison therefore stands only after passing both computational and governance verification.
claims.scope: Synthesizes the dual computational and governance qualifications required for defensible product comparisons across the wall case and three international frameworks.
caveats: The wall case illustrates pairing on a single climate indicator; real multi-indicator comparisons must additionally confront cross-category trade-offs, behavioral reuse rates, and review independence, examined next in Carrier-Bag Studies.

claims.text: Suppose a redesigned product uses less electricity during operation but requires more energy to manufacture. Determining whether the redesign actually improves environmental performance starts with two questions: do the original and redesigned products deliver the same service, and which activities expand or contract to provide it? The 2001 operational guide from the Center of Environmental Science at Leiden University (CML) uses this type of question to define the purpose of life cycle assessment (LCA). Measuring only an appliance's operating power or a component's mass answers only a partial question; evaluating the redesign as a whole requires tracing the links between production and use.
claims.scope: Functional comparison and burden shifting in CML 2001 Part 1, §2.1.
caveats: This general comparative framing does not constitute an environmental superiority judgment for any real product.

claims.text: Consider painting a wall. What the user requires is wall coverage meeting specified performance criteria, and paint is purchased to deliver that coverage. In the CML 2001 Part 2a guide (§2.3.4), the functional unit specifies the required coverage performance, the reference flow is expressed as the specified wall area covered using Paint A, and the required paint volume is recorded in the process data. By contrast, the European Commission Joint Research Center's International Reference Life Cycle Data System (ILCD) Handbook (2010, §6.4.1) presents two ways to formulate the reference flow in its own painting example: directly stating the covered wall area delivered by the paint, or stating the volume of paint required. Which formulation fits depends on product application, data structure, and how processes connect in software; whether area and volume can be interchanged depends on which step each quantity represents and how they relate. Differences in phrasing between these two guides do not by themselves establish conflicting normative rules.
claims.scope: Comparison of functional unit and reference flow formulations in CML 2001 Part 2a (§2.3.4) and ILCD 2010 (§6.4.1).
caveats: Does not establish a fixed cross-framework definition or infer normative contradiction from differing examples; terminological alignment depends on full definitions and study purpose.

claims.text: Once the shared service is defined, the analyst must decide which activities belong inside the system. The 1996 United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) guide warns that environmental burdens can shift from one life cycle stage to another, from one type of environmental problem to another, or from one location to another. It illustrates this with heavy-metal-bearing ash: incorporating the ash as a cement additive transfers the metals into a second product without necessarily immobilizing them. Bringing a recycling process inside the system boundary is therefore only the first step. Determining whether net burdens actually fall requires checking how the model represents the ash and its subsequent fate, and how omitting any downstream link could alter the conclusion. This example reflects practice at the time of the 1996 guide; whether later methods capture such transfers depends on the specific model used.
claims.scope: Integrative scope and omission example in UNEP 1996, Part I (pp. 7–9).
caveats: The cited omission reflects the 1996 guide's historical context and does not imply that all subsequent LCA models are unable to represent such transfers.

claims.text: Even with a broad system boundary, every model simplifies reality. The CML 2001 guide (Part 1, §§2.4–2.5) discusses linear modeling of activities alongside simplifications of spatial, temporal, and market dynamics. Similarly, the UNEP 1996 guide (pp. 40–41) distinguishes comparisons organized around a functional unit from site-specific analyses of actual facility pollution. Comparing resource demands for a shared service requires different information from estimating the risk a single facility poses to its surrounding community. Analysts should state how results will be used before checking whether omitted detail could change the answer; what extra insight a dynamic or regionalized model provides depends on which physical or economic relationships it actually retains.
claims.scope: Methodological boundaries and modeling simplifications in CML 2001 (Part 1, §§2.4–2.5) and UNEP 1996 (pp. 40–41).
caveats: Simplifications noted in historical guides are not permanent prohibitions against subsequent dynamic, regionalized, or other methodological extensions.

claims.text: Potential impact indicators show the consequences estimated under a particular model, but choosing among options requires further justification. As the CML 2001 guide notes (Part 1, §§2.4–2.5), scientific analysis still embeds technical assumptions and value choices and cannot replace decision-making itself. Interpreting results requires verifying the functional unit and checking whether the model represents where and when impacts occur. When selecting an alternative, analysts and decision-makers must separate differences estimated by the model from trade-offs that require value judgment. Because different impact methods treat time and space differently, numbers placed side by side in a single table must still be interpreted according to their underlying models.
claims.scope: Assumptions, potential impact indicators, and decision-support boundaries in CML 2001 Part 1 (§§2.4–2.5).
caveats: Reflects the scope of the CML 2001 guide and does not imply that all impact assessment methods share the same spatial or temporal treatment.

claims.text: Available evidence can sometimes pinpoint which activities drive a given impact while remaining unable to rank two alternatives overall. In its interpretation chapter, the 2006 U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) guide notes that uncertainty may prevent an overall ranking even while the study still clarifies how each option's impacts arise. Real-world decisions also weigh technical performance, cost, and social or political acceptability. A study can therefore identify the main contributors to an impact while keeping the overall ranking open; failing to distinguish two options does not establish that they are environmentally equivalent, which demands different evidence.
claims.scope: Interpretation checks and ranking limits in EPA 2006, Chapter 5 (pp. 54–58).
caveats: Does not equate an undetected difference with proven equivalence, nor substitute pedagogical guidance for real-world option selection.

claims.text: What a study should measure next depends on which step of the comparison remains unresolved. The ILCD Handbook (2010, Chapter 4 and §9.1) links iteration to information and precision requirements, using interpretation findings to re-examine earlier phases. Studies of long-term scenarios or emerging technologies may involve consequential differences that high uncertainty obscures; likewise, insufficient key data, staff resources, or budget cannot justify concluding that two options show no significant difference. Identifying whether the bottleneck lies in data, modeling, or resources defines what the next iteration should improve. Because the handbook addresses interpretation within selected study contexts, this guidance should not be read as a universal statistical criterion.
claims.scope: Iterative refinement and interpretation limits in ILCD 2010, Chapter 4 (pp. 25–28) and §9.1 (p. 285).
caveats: Requirements and explanations are bound to the 2010 ILCD Handbook and do not assert a single statistical criterion across all analytical contexts.

claims.text: This monograph follows that analytical sequence. After specifying the delivered service, it examines which activities and exchanges constitute the system; after compiling the inventory, it asks which consequences impact models can explain; and before choosing an option, it checks what level of judgment the data, assumptions, and trade-off rationales can support. Tracing evidence back through each step clarifies which conclusions hold and which questions remain open. This sequence organizes the analytical narrative of the monograph; individual standards' formal procedures must still be applied within their respective scopes.
claims.scope: Analytical sequence linking function, system connections, characterization coverage, and scope of conclusions.
caveats: This is an integrative analytical sequence, not a complete procedure for any formal standard, and it does not supply verified environmental conclusions.

claims.text: When comparing beverage bottles, glass and metal draw the eye first. Robert G. Hunt and colleagues instead asked how switching an entire packaging system alters resource inputs and environmental releases. Published by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) in 1974, Resource and Environmental Profile Analysis of Nine Beverage Container Alternatives (SW-91c) framed this comparison around packaging practices and solid waste. Transporting raw materials to factories, shipping filled bottles to retailers, and returning or disposing of used containers can all change with the container choice—making what happens after a bottle leaves the bottling plant just as consequential as what it is made of.
claims.scope: Title, foreword, and container-system scope of EPA SW-91c (1974).
caveats: Does not generalize the 1974 report's findings into environmental superiority claims for contemporary products or materials.

claims.text: Interpreting the 1974 report's energy totals requires reading its two volumes together. Volume I introduces the methodology and summarizes container comparisons across reuse and recycling scenarios; Volume II compiles process data and conversion factors by material system. Reconstructing what can be verified means first identifying the compared systems and reported totals in Volume I, then tracing supply activities and accounting denominators in Volume II. Volume numbers cited below and in the appendix Container Energy Verification refer to this two-volume report.
claims.scope: Two-volume structure of EPA SW-91c (1974) and citation convention used in this chapter.
caveats: The examined record is a single 185-page scan containing both volumes, not two independent studies.

claims.text: Begin with the task both containers must perform. The 1974 report records material and energy flows per unit mass of process output, assembles those data into container systems, and converts the results using container weights to a common beverage-delivery basis: supplying 1,000 liters of beer to consumers in 12-fluid-ounce containers. Process accounting establishes the inputs needed to produce a given mass of container, while the service basis determines how much of each activity is required. When two bottles differ in unit weight or reuse count, delivering the same volume of beer requires different quantities of newly manufactured glass.
claims.scope: Process basis and common beverage-delivery comparison basis in SW-91c Volume I (pp. 14–15).
caveats: Records the comparison basis actually used in the 1974 report rather than claiming the first historical appearance of the functional unit concept.
Documenting the comparison basis does not by itself verify equivalence across all product performance attributes or use conditions.

claims.text: A one-way glass bottle leaves the filling loop after a single use, so the next beverage delivery requires a new bottle. A returnable bottle is collected, washed, and refilled, allowing a single manufactured bottle to serve multiple deliveries. Accordingly, the 1974 report treats different reuse counts as distinct systems; interpreting any returnable-system result requires first checking its assumptions for the bottle, secondary packaging, and return logistics.
claims.scope: Definition of returnable and one-way container scenarios in SW-91c Volume I (pp. 1–2, 4, 14–15).
caveats: Does not infer actual reuse rates, loss rates, or environmental outcomes for any contemporary product.

claims.text: Consider two glass beer systems from the report. The ten-trip returnable system (10-RET) models off-premise consumption—beer bought for consumption away from the point of sale—with 10 bottle uses and 3 paper-carrier uses. The one-way glass system (OWG) represents conventional single-use glass bottles. Both use steel closures, but they differ in bottle weight, secondary packaging, new-bottle replenishment, and return handling. The sections below trace these differences step by step on a common beverage-delivery basis.
claims.scope: 10-RET and OWG off-premise beer systems in SW-91c (excluding 19-RET and rankings across other materials).
caveats: Three paper-carrier uses belong specifically to the 10-RET scenario; the five-trip bottle scenario with varying carrier reuse discussed later is a separate scenario.

claims.text: The accounting starts from 1,000,000 fillings of 12 fluid ounces of beer each. Here fluid ounces measure beverage volume, whereas ounces in the bottle-weight tables measure mass. Because a single returnable bottle can be filled repeatedly, the authors define trippage as the average number of uses N to determine how many new bottles must be supplied. Crucially, N includes the initial trip: an average of 10 uses means 1 initial filling plus 9 return refillings. The original tables do not report a bottle-lifetime distribution from this average.
claims.scope: Counting units and average trippage N in SW-91c Volume II (pp. 88–91, Table 29, Figure 4) and Volume I (pp. 19–21, 28, 30).
caveats: The trippage formula alone specifies neither return probabilities, breakage distributions, nor practically achievable reuse rates.

claims.text: Next, calculate the required mass of new bottles. The report works in short tons, where 1 short ton equals 2,000 lb. At the report's typical returnable bottle weight of 0.61 lb, 1,000,000 fillings correspond to 305 short tons of glass passing through filling; at 10 uses per bottle, new bottle manufacture equals 305 / 10 = 30.5 short tons. For one-way bottles at 0.41 lb each, new glass demand is 205 short tons. Volume II Table 6 prints 30 short tons for the 10-trip system; any calculation using that table value must note its difference from the exact formula result of 30.5 short tons.
claims.scope: New glass demand calculated from published bottle weights, 2,000 lb/short ton, and 1,000,000 fillings; does not recover undisclosed precision.
caveats: Bottle weights are the authors' typical values; the exact decimal figures shown reflect arithmetic on those printed inputs.

claims.text: Subtracting new bottle supply from total fillings isolates the return flow. Under 10-RET, 100,000 new returnable bottles still deliver 1,000,000 fillings. Volume II Figure 4 assigns 305 short tons to filling and 30.5 short tons each to new manufacture and final disposal, yielding a return flow of 305 − 30.5 = 274.5 short tons. These filling and return tonnages represent cumulative throughput across the delivery batch rather than a standing inventory of bottles in circulation at one instant. Dividing manufacturing mass by N does not mean every stage in the system scales by 1/N.
claims.scope: Mass-flow reconstruction for 1,000,000 fillings from SW-91c Volume II Figure 4 (pp. 88–91).
caveats: This mass balance does not determine transport distances, vehicle load factors, or consumer return behavior.

claims.text: Reusing existing bottles still consumes resources and transport. The 1974 study accounts for washing energy, cleaning chemicals, and backhaul transport returning empty bottles from retailers to the bottling plant. Closures, washing, and return haulage must each be scaled to their own activity count. Corrugated shipping cases must also be distinguished by role: cases carrying empty bottles from the glass plant serve a different stage from secondary packaging carrying filled bottles. For one-way bottles, incoming shipping cases are reused to ship out filled bottles, so new packaging demand must match the same case across both stages.
claims.scope: Packaging, washing, closure, and filling activity bases in SW-91c Volume II (pp. 56, 80, 82, 85–86, 88–91) and Volume I (p. 28).
caveats: Explains the quantity basis for each activity and does not claim a full independent recalculation of detergent use or transport routes.

claims.text: Reading historical reports also requires distinguishing methodological shorthand from itemized table entries. In its methodology section (Volume I, Chapter II, p. 9), SW-91c uses the term manufacture broadly to span the accounting scope from underground raw-material extraction through processing and transport to final container disposal. This does not mean factory-gate fabrication alone, nor does it mean that forming, transport, and disposal are collapsed into one row in the itemized tables. Interpreting subsequent tables and exclusions requires keeping the overall accounting scope distinct from individual process entries.
claims.scope: Explicit methodological usage of 'manufacture' in SW-91c Volume I, Chapter II (p. 9).
caveats: Does not claim that all 1970s studies used identical terminology or achieved complete life cycle coverage.

claims.text: What an indicator column measures determines what conclusions it can support. Although the report's summary refers broadly to water, the methodology actually records the volume of discharged process water while listing waterborne pollutants separately. Air emissions are tabulated by mass of each substance without damage weighting. Consequently, the water column reports wastewater discharge volume rather than water consumption, and air tables compare emitted masses of listed substances; assessing environmental damage requires additional models linking those releases to actual effects.
claims.scope: Parameter definitions and damage-quantification limits in SW-91c Volume I (pp. 9, 11–12).
caveats: Clarifying parameter definitions does not validate underlying inventory data or equate these 1974 metrics with modern life cycle impact assessment (LCIA) methods.

claims.text: The energy column traces process energy carriers back to primary resource requirements. Fuel factors include extraction, processing, transport, and combustion energy; electricity is converted to resource energy using a specified generation mix; and the energy value of certain organic materials is also included in the total. Reported energy totals therefore capture energy activities well beyond site meter readings. Estimating climate impacts, however, still requires emission inventories paired with an appropriate impact model.
claims.scope: Primary-resource energy accounting convention in the 1974 Resource and Environmental Profile Analysis (REPA), Volume I (pp. 11–14, 17) and Volume II (pp. 44–45, 49–50).
caveats: Applies specifically to the examined 1974 report and does not establish a universal energy indicator across all LCA methodologies.

claims.text: Electricity illustrates how background conventions shape energy totals. Volume II Table 4 lists 11.1 million British thermal units (Btu) of supply energy per 1,000 kilowatt-hours (kWh) of composite electricity, based on a U.S. generation mix labeled 1972 and specific energy-equivalence conventions for hydropower and nuclear generation. This factor does more than convert end-use electricity units: it computes primary resource demand under a chosen grid background. Changing the electricity mix, equivalence convention, or source vintage alters the meaning of the resulting figure.
claims.scope: Electricity generation mix and primary energy factor in SW-91c Volume II (§I.B, p. 49; Table 4, p. 50).
caveats: Follows the year printed in the table; p. 49 and Table 4 label the mix 1972 whereas Bibliography reference 78 cites 1970, and the underlying source vintage has not been independently verified or altered.

claims.text: Part of the glass-manufacturing energy demand can be independently recalculated. Process fuels and electricity are multiplied by supply-inclusive energy factors, combined with upstream inorganic materials on a common system basis, and then scaled by the mass of new glass required for beverage delivery. The appendix Container Energy Verification sets out these inputs, denominators, and equations in detail. Reconstructing the full container system from line items additionally requires packaging, filling, closures, disposal, and system transport.
claims.scope: Verification levels separating glass manufacturing, the system glass branch, and full reported system totals.
caveats: This synthesis introduces no new numerical inputs or outputs and does not claim reproduction of the complete original computer program.

claims.text: The glass branch explains only part of the gap between the two systems; overall totals still come from the report's summary tables. Per 1,000,000 12-fluid-ounce fillings, Volume II Tables 7 and 13 report 1,717 million Btu of process energy, 308 million Btu of transport energy, and 1 million Btu of material resource energy for 10-RET, summing to 2,026 million Btu; the corresponding OWG figures are 5,461, 574, and 1, summing to 6,036 million Btu. These are the report's published whole-system totals. Because the glass branch recalculated in Container Energy Verification covers only a subset of activities, it cannot be cited as an independent derivation of the full system totals.
claims.scope: Published system energy totals and displayed subtotals in SW-91c Volume II Tables 7 (p. 57) and 13 (p. 64).
caveats: Summing displayed subtotals checks only internal arithmetic among reported figures and does not independently verify all underlying process inputs.

claims.text: To compare energy demand per 1,000 liters of beer, convert 1,000,000 fillings into beverage volume. Using the report's printed constants of 0.02957 L per fluid ounce and 1,055 J per Btu, 1,000,000 12-fluid-ounce fillings equal 354,840 L. Volume II (§I.D, p. 51) also supplies a combined conversion factor of 0.002973 to convert million Btu per 12 million fluid ounces directly into gigajoules (GJ) per 1,000 L. Multiplying 2,026 and 6,036 by 0.002973 gives 6.023298 and 17.945028 GJ/1,000 L, which round to 6.02 and 17.9—matching the summary values printed in Volume I.
claims.scope: Normalization of reported totals using published conversion factors in SW-91c Volume II (§I.D, p. 51); does not recover undisclosed precision.
caveats: Volume I p. 19 separately lists 2,817 12-oz containers per 1,000 L; this check explicitly uses the p. 51 published decimals and combined factor rather than treating printed numbers as infinite-precision identities.

claims.text: Three distinct verification checks must be kept separate. Converting published totals to a 1,000-liter basis checks units and the comparison denominator; recalculating from process inputs and energy factors checks glass manufacturing and its upstream chain; and summing all itemized activities on compatible bases is what tests full system reconstruction from the ground up. Agreement in the first two checks does not substitute for the third, and retaining extra decimal places during recalculation adds no precision beyond the original measurements.
claims.scope: Analytical distinction among three levels of historical reconstruction in the 1974 container case.
caveats: Unreconstructed components do not invalidate verified arithmetic, nor does partial agreement establish reproduction of the complete original model.

claims.text: Now test whether the itemized table reassembles the OWG total. Volume II Table 8 sets 1 short ton of the one-way glass container system as its common basis, organizing each activity to match the material quantities required for that system. The eight glass and upstream inorganic-material items listed in Container Energy Verification sum to 18.523 million Btu; adding disposal (0.139), closures (0.505), system transport (1.500), filling (0.683), and packaging (7.752) brings the 13 displayed items to 29.102 million Btu per short ton of system basis. Because every OWG filling uses one new bottle, scaling by the printed bottle-weight mass of 205 short tons per 1,000,000 fillings yields 5,965.910 million Btu—70.09 million Btu below the 6,036 million Btu reported in Tables 7 and 13. Following the published system names and bases, whole-table assembly does not close exactly from these displayed inputs, though the discrepancy alone does not prove an error in the original report.
claims.scope: Itemized assembly check for OWG using fixed 205 short tons and displayed coefficients from SW-91c Volume II Table 8 (p. 59).
caveats: Does not establish a confirmed error in the 1974 report; differing table bases, undisclosed mass precision, or other inputs may account for the gap.

claims.text: Explaining the 70.09 million Btu gap requires knowing what data the original authors actually entered. SW-91c drew on published statistics, unpublished reports, and proprietary industry data used by Midwest Research Institute (MRI) for estimation, and the authors themselves noted that actual trippage is difficult to determine accurately. Holding the printed bottle weight fixed, the appendix Container Energy Verification tests how much of the gap displayed-coefficient rounding alone could explain. Because unprinted mass precision, transport attribution, and program inputs remain unknown, a single aggregate difference cannot uniquely invert those modeling choices; tuning one parameter until the numbers match does not recover the original data or code.
claims.scope: Reconstruction boundary and source provenance limits of the published 1974 record (SW-91c Volume II p. 90; Bibliography pp. 175–177).
caveats: Citing references to proprietary records does not imply access to them, and the unavailability of original computer code is not evidence of scientific invalidity.

claims.text: The 1974 report also varied paper-carrier reuse independently of bottle reuse. Holding bottle trippage constant at 5 uses, it reported system energy of 12 GJ/1,000 L when the paper carrier is used once, 9.0 GJ/1,000 L when used twice, and 8 GJ/1,000 L when used three times. These three discrete scenario outputs from the original authors demonstrate that packaging assumptions materially shift system comparisons, but they are not independently verified full-model outputs from the appendix's local reconstruction, nor do three points define a general formula for arbitrary reuse counts.
claims.scope: Paper-carrier reuse sensitivity at fixed five-trip bottle use in SW-91c Volume I (p. 29, referring to p. 28 scenario definitions).
caveats: Printed precision varies across the three original points; fitting a curve to three points neither recovers the original program nor supports contemporary packaging recommendations.

claims.text: Comparing five-trip returnable (5-RET) and 10-RET systems highlights why multiple assumptions must be separated. The 5-RET system assumes 5 bottle uses and 1 paper-carrier use, whereas 10-RET assumes 10 bottle uses and 3 carrier uses. Because both bottle and packaging reuse change simultaneously, the entire energy gap between 5-RET and 10-RET cannot be attributed solely to bottle reuse. The separate three-point sensitivity holds bottle reuse fixed at 5 and varies only carrier reuse. The two sets of figures answer different questions—one compares two bundled systems, the other isolates carrier reuse within a given model—so each result must be reported with its comparison conditions.
claims.scope: Conditional comparison and attribution of system differences within SW-91c Volume I (pp. 19–21, 28–30).
caveats: Does not identify real-world market causal effects; the source model's supply, return, and technology conditions still govern every result.

claims.text: After comparing the two systems, check what both leave out. The report's summary explicitly excludes litter, waste heat, and carbon dioxide. Consumer shopping trips to carry beverages home from the store are also omitted on the grounds that a shopping trip serves multiple purposes. The first group of exclusions limits which environmental stressors the study tracks, while omitting consumer trips limits which activities enter the system boundary. Even when two systems share the same beverage-delivery task, both types of boundary choice must be stated explicitly.
claims.scope: Explicit environmental and activity exclusions in SW-91c Volume I (pp. 1–2, 4, 17–18).
caveats: Reflects the 1974 study's conventions and does not prescribe the same exclusions for contemporary container studies.

claims.text: Including a process in the inventory does not guarantee that the data represent it well. Where foreign activity data were unavailable, the 1974 authors substituted U.S. data, and the study did not assess the ecological burdens imposed on specific local sites. Even after confirming that an emission belongs to a process inside the system, two further evidentiary questions remain: whether the chosen data represent the actual activity, and whether emitted mass characterizes site-specific environmental consequences. Broad life cycle coverage cannot substitute for either check.
claims.scope: Analytical distinction among system scope, data representativeness, and site-specific impact boundaries drawn from SW-91c Volume I (pp. 9, 17–18).
caveats: Organizing these limits into three questions is an interpretive framing rather than a modern standard classification from the original report.

claims.text: The 1974 EPA report turned a shared beverage-delivery task into auditable process accounting: trippage governs new-bottle replenishment, fuel and electricity factors convert site inputs to primary resource energy, and totals normalize to a common service. Recalculation clarifies which relationships can be verified from published inputs while pinpointing the exact 70.09 million Btu gap between itemized assembly and the published OWG total. Those results support comparing container systems under the report's 1974 conditions, but deciding whether national policy should prioritize container intervention requires knowing how large those differences are relative to broader consumption and environmental problems.
claims.scope: Integrative conclusion linking the 1974 container accounting case to policy-level evaluation.
caveats: Does not provide independent verification of the complete original program, all environmental indicators, or contemporary commercial products.

claims.text: Delivering the same beverage can involve very different bottling systems, yet proposing national policy requires explaining why government should intervene specifically in beverage containers. The Research Triangle Institute (RTI) report The Beverage Container Problem: Analysis and Recommendations (EPA-R2-72-059) evaluated policy options to advise the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). Its title page is dated September 1972, while the examined copy carries an April 1973 reprint notice reproducing the body text as received with added cover and front matter—two dates reflecting distinct publication events for the same study. EPA approved publication of the report, while the policy recommendations remain those of the authors.
claims.scope: Title, reprint provenance, and policy-evaluation purpose of RTI's EPA-R2-72-059 (September 1972; reprinted April 1973).
caveats: EPA approval for publication does not mean all recommendations became agency policy; only the cited policy framing is examined here.

claims.text: The RTI report examines resource use, solid waste, and litter in turn, judging each against its national scale. Litter—excluded from the 1974 container inventory—is precisely one of the problems policy may need to address here. Reading the two reports side by side also separates two counting objects: how many beverage servings are sold versus how many new bottles are manufactured, since reuse lets one bottle cover multiple fillings. How much resource a switch saves per beverage delivery and what share of national resource use or waste that change represents require separate accounting.
claims.scope: Policy rationales and counting objects in RTI 1972 (Chapter 1, pp. 2–4; Chapter 2, p. 7) contrasted with SW-91c (1974).
caveats: The closing distinction is an analytical framing of problem scales, not an empirical judgment on current policy priorities.

claims.text: If switching to returnable containers lowers what consumers spend on beverages, what else will they buy with the savings? After citing estimates of potential energy savings from returnable containers, RTI (§2.2.5 and continuation, pp. 14–17) considers the energy demanded by other consumer spending. The report neither calculates the energy required for those other goods nor observes how consumers actually reallocate spending; instead, it argues that estimating net energy change must look beyond container production and use. Quantifying economy-wide net effects requires separate evidence on how household spending responds.
claims.scope: Consumer re-spending argument in RTI 1972, Chapter 2 (§2.2.5, pp. 14–17).
caveats: Does not treat the authors' proposed mechanism as measured behavioral response or retroactively assign a modern consequential-LCA definition to it.

claims.text: To trace links between consumer spending and industrial production, RTI drew on input–output data reflecting the 1963 U.S. industrial structure. Its Table 5 maps off-premise food, bottled and canned soft drinks, and related categories to supplying industries, reporting how many dollars of direct and indirect industrial output are required per dollar of consumer expenditure. Using such figures requires stating both the consumption category and the data year. Linking monetary input–output tables to process accounting organized per beverage delivery further requires specifying the service and physical activities represented by each dollar spent before tracing physical resources and emissions.
claims.scope: Monetary input–output unit and 1963 structural basis in RTI 1972 (p. 15 and Table 5 notes).
caveats: Does not reconstruct the original input–output tables or the complete monetary demand relationships in Appendix D.

claims.text: In Table 5, RTI compares soft drinks against broader food-consumption categories; as the authors interpret those data, resource requirements appear to differ only slightly. Yet the table reflects 1963 industrial structure. By 1969—the period the report discusses—the share of returnable bottles in soft-drink fillings had declined, leading the authors to suggest that resource demands may have risen accordingly. Because that reasoning rests on monetary spending-to-industry relationships, establishing the physical resources required to deliver an identical beverage service still demands process accounting on a shared service basis.
claims.scope: Qualitative comparison in RTI 1972 (pp. 15–16), its 1963/1969 structural qualification, and its citation boundary.
caveats: The original authors explicitly noted they had not conducted an intensive comparison; this qualitative reading is neither an equivalence test nor a modern empirical finding.
This excerpt does not independently verify the 1963 input–output dataset, full Appendix D tables, or primary 1969 market-share data cited by the report.

claims.text: RTI ultimately ranked the social cost of litter as the primary rationale for government intervention, followed by solid waste, and did not use resource or energy consumption to define the beverage-container policy problem. Later sections address resources and energy more generally through supply–demand relationships and rates of use. That priority ranking reflects the authors' policy judgment and cannot be deduced from Table 5 alone; whether their recommendations were adopted and what effects followed require separate historical evidence.
claims.scope: Historical policy problem framing in RTI 1972 (pp. 3–4, 17), not a contemporary policy recommendation.
caveats: Documents how the original authors framed the policy problem without validating their policy comparisons, adoption history, or actual environmental outcomes.
Historical resource judgments and their reference years cannot be converted directly into present-day resource facts or policy advice.

claims.text: The two reports thus serve distinct judgments. The 1974 EPA container study holds beverage delivery constant to compare physical container systems under explicit reuse assumptions, whereas RTI's 1972 national policy analysis weighs what consumers pay to avoid returning empties, competing household expenditures, and public environmental costs such as litter. Choosing policy purely on energy totals would overlook several of those concerns. Clarifying what information each study provides is far more useful for matching evidence to a decision than lining up their conclusions chronologically.
claims.scope: Contrast of decision questions and analytical levels between RTI 1972 and SW-91c 1974.
caveats: Synthesizes the difference in analytical framing without claiming that subsequent empirical evidence validated either report's conclusions.

claims.text: The 1974 report also records a concrete reason why priorities were re-evaluated at the time. Referring to the late-1973 energy crisis (Volume I, p. 33), the authors noted that such disruptions shift the relative importance assigned to different impacts, prompting closer examination of total energy demand and its sources. Because the report already tracked multiple environmental parameters, what shifted was which issues readers and decision-makers prioritized most urgently. That passage supports this specific link within the report, without explaining the broader relationship between the energy crisis and the subsequent development of the entire field.
claims.scope: Contemporaneous discussion of the late-1973 energy crisis in SW-91c Volume I (p. 33).
caveats: Does not use this passage to establish global methodological origins or a complete causal history of the energy crisis's effect on LCA.

claims.text: Together, these two early studies make concrete several core analytical tasks: defining a comparable service, tracing linked activities and resource demands, and examining how exclusions and alternative spending affect policy judgment. Those tasks provide a baseline for comparing how later assessment frameworks organize a study; determining who influenced whom or who invented a given method first requires historical documentation able to prove those links. The next chapter, Assessment Frameworks and Analytical Steps, examines how calculation, evaluation, improvement, and result use are structured across formal frameworks.
claims.scope: Comparison objects, activity links, and policy uses across RTI 1972 and SW-91c 1974; not a comprehensive history.
caveats: Does not constitute a complete history, proof of global firsts, attribution to a single inventor, or an established genealogy of influence.

claims.text: In his 2002 article, Qihong Sun defines cleaner production as a preventive strategy applied continuously to production processes, products, and services, and proposes using life cycle assessment (LCA) to identify, diagnose, and evaluate improvement opportunities. Using cleaner-production audits as an example, the paper recommends examining on-site facility operations alongside upstream raw materials and downstream product use and waste fate, extending the scope from raw-material acquisition through production and use to final disposal. Within this framing, cleaner production sets the preventive objective while LCA helps pinpoint where interventions may matter most.
claims.scope: Conceptual framing and proposed role of LCA in cleaner production in Sun (2002, §§2.1–2.3, 4.1–4.5, 5).
caveats: Reflects Qihong Sun's 2002 exposition of LCA's purpose and does not automatically establish current regulatory requirements or verified performance gains for specific products.

claims.text: An analysis sufficient to flag hotspots for internal investigation may not support public claims. Sun (2002, §2.2) classifies LCA by technical complexity into conceptual, simplified (or streamlined), and detailed types, explicitly warning that conceptual LCA should not be used for marketing promotion or public communication. In practice, users must define what information a decision requires before checking whether the chosen level of analysis supplies it. This three-tier classification belongs to Sun's article, and calling a study detailed does not exempt its specific results from verification.
claims.scope: Interpretive boundary of the three-level technical complexity classification in Sun (2002, §2.2).
caveats: References to International Organization for Standardization (ISO) concepts in the article do not substitute for authorized standard clauses.
Adopts only the article's complexity typology without establishing a unified cross-guideline classification.

claims.text: Sun (2002, §3.2) surveys contemporaneous Chinese efforts in standard adoption, funded research, international cooperation, eco-labeling, packaging, manufacturing, and audits. The four national standards under adoption stood at different stages: the article states that Environmental Management — Life Cycle Assessment — Principles and Framework and Environmental Management — Life Cycle Assessment — Goal and Scope Definition and Inventory Analysis had already been issued, while the remaining two were expected to be issued in 2002. These statements record progress as reported at the time; when the latter two standards were actually issued and how widely the cited applications spread nationally require independent verification.
claims.scope: Contemporaneous status report of Chinese LCA standards and activities in Sun (2002, §3.2).
caveats: Does not confirm that expected milestones were subsequently completed; specific historical events require contemporaneous standard or project records.
Examples of funding and cooperation do not verify the underlying methods or project conclusions.

claims.text: Sun's proposed applications extend analysis upstream to suppliers and downstream to product and waste fate. Specifically, the paper recommends that cleaner-production audits trace upstream raw materials and downstream product and waste flows, that eco-design cover the full product life cycle, and that eco-industrial park assessments connect intra-park production with external supply and disposal, alongside recycling and recovery management. Such analyses can screen activities for priority investigation, but demonstrating how much environmental performance actually improves after implementation requires before-and-after or controlled comparative data, which the article does not provide.
claims.scope: Application prospects versus empirical outcome evidence in Sun (2002, §§4–5).
caveats: Does not deny that individual projects may succeed; bounds only the evidence actually presented in the 2002 article.
Demonstrating real-world gains requires product or process inventories, explicit comparison premises, and verification records.

claims.text: Turning application prospects into decision-ready studies requires data, funding, and foundational methodology, all of which Sun's conclusion identifies as still lacking domestically in 2002. Crucially, the "maturity phase" cited in the article's opening (§1) refers to the international development of LCA methodology, whereas the conclusion (§5) evaluates domestic prerequisites for local application. Recognizing that these two assessments address different objects clarifies why the author proposed a domestic development agenda, without constituting an overall judgment on a country's capabilities.
claims.scope: Distinction between international methodological maturity (§1) and domestic application prerequisites (§5) in Sun (2002).
caveats: Does not establish early-origin priority claims or judge the quality of all domestic research.
Reflects a brief 2002 commentary by Qihong Sun rather than a comprehensive national historical survey.

claims.text: On that basis, Sun (2002, §5) recommends importing and digesting international methods, developing locally adapted methods and datasets, and conducting applied research and demonstrations in cleaner-production audits, eco-design, waste management, and eco-industrial systems. Together, these arguments separate two questions: what LCA can help investigate, and what infrastructure is needed to carry out those investigations—work that remained underway when the paper appeared in 2002. With historical origins and framework divisions established, Part II (Service and Inventory) turns to functional reference—distinguishing functional units, declared units, reference flows, and comparability thresholds—before examining process networks, flow exchanges, and hybrid inventory boundaries.
claims.scope: Methodological, data, and applied-research agenda in Sun (2002, §5) and transition to Part II.
caveats: Explains only the work directions proposed in 2002 without verifying subsequent project execution, nationwide adoption, or realized environmental gains.
These historical recommendations are not equivalent to current institutional or regulatory requirements.

claims.text: Quantifying a set of emissions is only the first step; analysts must also estimate the associated environmental consequences to identify where improvements are worth pursuing. Once designers propose changes, those modifications must in turn be checked for their system-wide effects before recommending action. Guidance issued by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), and the Center of Environmental Science at Leiden University (CML) organizes these analytical tasks in different ways. This chapter compares those assessment frameworks through the outputs each phase produces.
claims.scope: Discussion of phase responsibilities and outputs in EPA (1993), UNEP (1996), CML (2001), and EPA (2006); does not constitute a complete intellectual lineage or current universal rules.

claims.text: Research topics raised at workshops, analytical components in technical reports, and operational steps in guidance manuals are easily collapsed into a single framework diagram in hindsight. Tracing when a given element emerged requires first distinguishing the nature of each record: workshop notes show what organizers placed on the agenda, operational guides specify how practitioners should conduct a study, and later pedagogical diagrams often compress several arrangements into an accessible overview. Available records document different ways of organizing inventory analysis, impact assessment, problem definition, and interpretation, but they cannot establish whether those arrangements share a single point of origin.
claims.scope: Distinction among historical document genres—workshops, reports, methodological components, and pedagogical classifications—in early institutional LCA literature.
caveats: Does not assert a global origin, individual inventor, or complete lineage of influence.

claims.text: A contemporaneous project record illustrates why document metadata must be read carefully. The March 1991 draft of the EPA report Pollution Prevention Research: Strategic Plan notes that the Society of Environmental Toxicology and Chemistry (SETAC) held a technical framework workshop on August 18–23, 1990, aimed at compiling terminology, reviewing the state of methodology and case studies, and setting research priorities. That project page records the workshop's mandate and dates, yet omits its venue. Moreover, the draft's date, the workshop's date, and the publication dates of subsequent reports are distinct facts and cannot substitute for one another.
claims.scope: Single project entry in the March 1991 draft of the EPA Strategic Plan.
caveats: This page neither names the venue nor proves that this was the first workshop, and it cannot substitute for the published workshop proceedings.

claims.text: In February 1993, the EPA published Life-Cycle Assessment: Inventory Guidelines and Principles (EPA/600/R-92/245), which directly addresses how a life cycle assessment (LCA) study is structured. The report presents inventory, impact, and improvement analysis as three core components alongside goal definition and scoping activities, while noting that some practitioners treat scoping as a fourth component and allowing the components to complement one another. Which division proves more useful depends on how effectively it helps analysts complete the required work.
claims.scope: Introduction and Overview of EPA/600/R-92/245 (February 1993).
caveats: The title-page publication date is distinct from the final drafting period; scanned pagination and figure optical character recognition (OCR) may limit exact locator precision.

claims.text: In the 1993 EPA guide, each of the three analytical components produces a distinct output: inventory analysis quantifies resource requirements and environmental releases, impact analysis estimates the potential consequences of those stressors, and improvement analysis identifies and evaluates opportunities to reduce environmental burdens. An inventory reports emission quantities, whereas impact analysis must explain what environmental consequences those emissions may cause. That distinction explains why inventory and impact analysis cannot be collapsed into a single step.
claims.scope: Phase responsibilities and outputs in EPA (1993), UNEP (1996), CML (2001), and EPA (2006); does not constitute a complete lineage or current universal prescription.

claims.text: Analysis can also loop back to earlier stages. The 1993 EPA guide notes that when a study's goal calls for interpreting impacts, scoping must prepare the corresponding inventory data from the outset. Inventory results may likewise reveal opportunities to cut material use or releases, prompting analysts to revise the goal, scope, and data. Although later frameworks separated interpretation into its own phase, this early guide already described iterative returns to prior work explicitly.
