A factory knows how much it spends annually on maintenance but lacks a process-level maintenance inventory; linking that expenditure to an economic input–output (IO) table estimates upstream maintenance activities from the sector's average input structure. A second factory does not even know which purchases were omitted and consults a comparable sector's input profile to flag potential gaps—yet that sector table may also include steel and electricity already measured directly. The first case starts from a known transaction that can be traced; the second requires checking both whether a transaction occurred and whether it is already counted.
claims.scope: Distinction between modeled process feedback loops and omitted supporting activities.

claims.text: Economic IO tables trace monetary transactions across broad supply chains, but sector-average input recipes may fail to represent a specific product. Suh et al. identify several sources of bias: heterogeneous products and technologies are aggregated into a single sector, price fluctuations alter monetary transaction values, imported goods may be modeled with domestic technology, reference years may diverge from the studied system, and environmental satellite accounts may be incomplete. Identifying which sector receives a payment is therefore only the first step; analysts must still verify whether that sector's average input structure represents the production in question.
claims.scope: Assessment of IO methods and data in the Suh (2004) dissertation reprint; not an evaluation of specific current databases.
caveats: The second-order truncation demonstration in the source rests on strong explicit assumptions and should not be generalized as a universal error magnitude for real-world inventories.

claims.text: How modeling responsibilities are divided between process data and economic IO tables defines the architecture of a hybrid inventory. Suh et al. distinguish three main forms: tiered hybrid analysis combines detailed process data with IO background data as separate tiers; input–output-based hybrid analysis disaggregates target economic sectors; and integrated hybrid analysis couples both accounts within a single mathematical framework. All three architectures must specify which supply relationships remain in the process system, which are assigned to economic sectors, and how the two sides connect.
claims.scope: Three hybrid approaches and their coverage relationships in Section 4 of the Suh (2004) dissertation reprint; the closing sentence is an analytical synthesis.
caveats: This historical taxonomy is not an exhaustive catalog of all subsequent hybrid life cycle assessment (LCA) methods.

claims.text: Where process and economic boundaries overlap, recording the same activity on both sides causes double counting. In a tiered hybrid case reviewed by Suh et al., international transport and national energy matrices overlapped without a satisfactory resolution. Integrated hybrid analysis attempts to remove commodity flows already represented in the process system and reconnect them through explicit boundary links. Verifying any subtraction requires tracing the same underlying activity across both accounts to confirm that both actually recorded it.
claims.scope: Account of the transport case and integrated hybrid method as reported in the Suh (2004) dissertation reprint; not an independent recalculation.
caveats: This summarizes the reprinted text's report of the transport case and integrated method and does not verify that any particular software implements double-counting subtraction correctly.

claims.text: In a companion single-author study, Suh illustrates how the two accounts connect using a hypothetical toaster that delivers a functional demand of 1,000 slices of toast over its use life. The process side tracks steel, electricity, toaster manufacturing, bread toasting, and waste treatment; the economic side tracks the monetary outputs of agriculture, mining, manufacturing, construction, finance, and other goods and services. Although both blocks serve the same final demand, each retains its own physical or monetary units—kilograms, kilowatt-hours, and US dollars.
claims.scope: Functional demand and economic system structure in Suh's single-author 2004 paper (read via dissertation Chapter III).

claims.text: Modeling waste treatment first requires choosing what flow is being accounted for. In a physical-flow convention, the use phase outputs waste and the treatment process receives it; in a service-flow convention, the treatment process supplies a waste-treatment service and the use phase demands that service. Suh's integrated example adopts the service convention, reversing the signs on both sides together. Either convention can describe the same treatment operation, but changing the row label without reversing the signs accordingly alters the activity required by the balance equations.
claims.scope: Supply-and-demand orientation of waste-treatment services versus physical waste flows.

claims.text: Begin by tracing purchases from the process system to economic sectors. Suh divides monetary purchases not covered by the process model during a steady-state reference period by each process's activity volume over that same period to form the upstream cut-off matrix Cᵘ. Here, activity volume is counted in units of the process's reference basis—for example, producing 1 kg of steel counts as one unit—rather than as equipment start-ups. Each column of Cᵘ corresponds to a process and each row to a background commodity, expressed in currency per unit of process reference. In the toaster example, producing 1 kg of steel requires purchasing USD 0.1 each from the mining and manufacturing sectors. Purchase valuations must match the price basis of the economic table.
claims.scope: Normalization of the upstream cut-off matrix per unit-operation reference basis of each process; does not denote equipment start-up counts.

claims.text: Next, ask what economic sectors purchase from the process system. Suh divides the physical quantities of functional flows received by each sector by that sector's monetary output to form the downstream cut-off matrix Cᵈ, expressed in physical units per currency unit of sectoral output. In the toaster example, each USD 1 of manufacturing output requires 0.01 kg of steel, 0.08 kWh of electricity, and 0.05 kg of waste-treatment service from the process side. When background sectors expand output, they draw more heavily on these process outputs, which in turn increases process purchases from the background economy—creating two-way feedback.
claims.scope: Downstream cut-off matrix expressed as physical quantities of process outputs per unit of monetary sectoral output.

claims.text: Let s denote the vector of process activities (in each process's reference units) and x the vector of background commodity outputs (in monetary units). Matrix P records each process's net supply of functional flows per unit operation (outputs positive, inputs negative), and matrix R records background inputs required per currency unit of sectoral output. The process balance reads Ps − Cᵈx = y: after deducting physical outputs consumed by background sectors, the remainder satisfies external final demand y. The background balance reads x − Rx − Cᵘs = 0: sectoral output covers intra-background and process purchases, with no separate external demand assigned to the background block. Provided coefficients are fixed and the combined block matrix is invertible, the system solves simultaneously for s and x.
claims.scope: Row units and solvability conditions of the coupled hybrid balance system.

claims.text: Environmental emissions are computed only after activity levels are solved. Direct CO₂ intensities per unit process operation multiply s, while direct background intensities per currency unit of output multiply x; both blocks can be summed only after conversion to kilograms of the same elementary flow. If steelmaking, electricity generation, and waste treatment are modeled explicitly on the process side, their direct emissions must be removed from the background environmental accounts. Balancing the technological flow equations does not by itself verify that emissions have not been counted twice.
claims.scope: Activity scaling and block-by-block aggregation of direct environmental interventions.

claims.text: The toaster example demonstrates why hybrid analysis cannot simply append a background total to a standalone process inventory. In Equation (7) of Suh's paper, one use cycle delivers 1,000 slices of toast and directly emits 1 kg CO₂; once steelmaking, electricity generation, and related upstream processes are linked, the author reports a process-based inventory of 18.1 kg CO₂. Coupling the two-way linkages raises the total to 30.015 kg CO₂—20.027 kg from the process block and 9.988 kg from the background economy. Because the toast row of Cᵈ is zero, the additional process burden arises entirely from background demand for steel, electricity, and waste-treatment services. Simply adding 18.1 and 9.988 omits the extra process activity induced by the background economy. All figures belong strictly to the author's hypothetical system.
claims.scope: Pedagogical 1,000-slice toaster example and its process and background contributions in Suh (2004).

claims.text: Even when the coupled equations are well defined, whether analysts actually need data on economic-sector purchases from individual processes depends on what the process dataset represents. In a 2004 working paper, Peters and Hertwich distinguish two cases: a process system that collectively represents only a specified functional unit versus a modular database in which every unit process can independently serve external demand. In the first case, downstream feedback tracks only how much of that same service is purchased by background activities triggered by the original demand—for instance, toast made on that toaster model for background employees' lunches, rather than all toast economy-wide. Judging such consumer-product feedbacks to be small in many cases, the authors suggest setting Cᵈ to zero under that premise. In the second case, identifying which processes supply each sector requires far more data and raises collection costs. Practical databases typically fall between the two extremes.
claims.scope: Distinction in the Peters and Hertwich (2004) working paper between fixed functional-unit systems and modular databases where any process can serve external demand.
caveats: Detailed arguments are drawn from the 2004 NTNU working paper; the 2006 journal comment of the same title has a distinct publication identity whose item-by-item correspondence remains to be verified.

claims.text: The working paper tests an alternative feedback assumption in which every economic sector purchases 0.01 slices of toast per USD 1 of output. Although the text states that this applies to every sector, Equation (6) displays only five columns without explaining how they map onto Suh's six economic sectors. Keeping external demand at 1,000 slices, the authors report about 0.0632 slices of induced internal demand and total emissions of 27.2369 kg CO₂ with feedback versus 27.2352 kg CO₂ with Cᵈ set to zero. The narrow gap confirms that feedback is negligible under that toast-service coefficient, but this result cannot be transferred to Suh's original example, which tracks downstream demand for steel, electricity, and waste treatment. Peters and Hertwich also reserve an exception for structural changes—such as major shifts in power generation—where sectoral demand for process outputs still warrants investigation.
claims.scope: Comparison in the Peters and Hertwich (2004) working paper between toast-row-only feedback and a zero downstream block.
caveats: Slices are modeled as continuously divisible activity units; 0.0632 is the reported induced internal demand while external functional demand remains 1,000 slices.

Text on page 4 applies 0.01 slices/USD to every sector, whereas Equation (6) displays five columns against Suh's six-sector economic block. Applying the coefficient across all six sectors reproduces the rounded page 5 results, though the column-count discrepancy remains.

claims.text: Deciding whether to include downstream feedback and preventing double counting when it is included are separate issues. As Agez et al. note in their supporting information, if an economic table already represents a process technology and sectoral purchases from the process side are then linked into the model, the existing coverage within the corresponding economic sector must be removed. Setting Cᵈ to zero merely omits that linkage; keeping the linkage still requires subtracting the overlapping side.
claims.scope: Distinction in Agez et al. Supporting Information S1 between omitting the downstream link and removing background overlap when retaining it.
caveats: Based on the two-page conceptual discussion in Agez et al. Supporting Information S1, which provides no pre-subtraction transaction or direct-emission ledger for a concrete economy; this claim does not verify empirical accuracy or specific account subtractions.

claims.text: Constructing the residual background coefficient matrix R requires returning to annual national accounts. Suh first aligns process flows to an annual basis, identifies monetary transactions and intermediate sectors, and maps functional flows to commodities and processes to industries. The use table must adjust three categories of already-covered flows: intra-process transactions, process sales to economic sectors, and process purchases from economic sectors. The supply (make) table removes the explicitly modeled production, and the environmental account removes direct interventions from those same activities. Only then is the residual background recalculated under the chosen technology assumption. Which expenditures are deleted, how much output is removed, and how emission intensity per currency unit shifts must each be traced in its respective account.
claims.scope: Adjusting annual supply, use, and emission accounts before deriving residual background coefficients.
caveats: Equation (A7) in the dissertation reprint writes the diagonal price matrix to the left of the mapped production matrix, which is defined with industries in rows and commodities in columns; axis correspondence must be verified before applying it to general supply tables. The small worked ledger below separates each known transaction explicitly by product, unit price, and supplier.

claims.text: Suh's toaster paper publishes the post-subtraction coefficients: Equations (28)–(32), combined with process emission intensities and final demand, are sufficient to reproduce Equation (33). However, the paper does not publish the pre-subtraction supply, use, mapping, price, and emission ledgers. Moreover, page 57 of the dissertation reprint states that upstream purchases are valued in producer prices, whereas page 58 states that economic coefficients use consumer prices, leaving the reconciliation between the two valuation bases undocumented. Reproducing the published total confirms internal arithmetic consistency given those coefficients, but auditing the subtraction and price conversion requires examining actual transactions and the valuation rules on both sides.
claims.scope: Reproducibility scope of the published toaster coefficients and unresolved price-basis documentation.

claims.text: To see exactly how a single transaction gets counted twice, consider a ledger that records both buyer and seller for every exchange. Returning to the smooth-substrate Paint A option from Wall Service Comparison, isolate its electricity requirement: painting 100 m² of smooth wall twice over ten years consumes 5 kg of Paint A per coat, and producing 1 kg of paint requires 2 kWh of electricity, totaling 20 kWh. Suppose generator F supplies this electricity, and we compute the CO₂ inventory of the power-supply system from the annual accounts of three suppliers. The wall schedule fixes only the required electricity delivery, and the resulting inventory covers solely the modeled power-supply activities; all transactions, technologies, regional scope, prices, and emissions below are pedagogical model assumptions.
claims.scope: Fixed electricity sub-demand derived from the smooth-wall Paint A option.

claims.text: Place all three suppliers in the same steady-state reference year, assuming that year's technologies and relative prices apply to the electricity delivery, with monetary values measured in currency units (CU). Two regional electricity generators, F and G, each produce 100 kWh/year and sell at a uniform producer price of 1 CU/kWh; a service supplier, S, produces 100 CU/year. Annual direct emissions are 40 kg CO₂ for F, 120 kg CO₂ for G, and 30 kg CO₂ for S. The annual accounts supply unit input and emission coefficients, while total demand from the ten-year wall plan remains 20 kWh rather than being multiplied by ten. The model assumes fixed-proportion scaling and omits taxes, trade margins, imports, transmission losses, capital goods, and co-products.
claims.scope: Hypothetical steady-state annual ledger: suppliers, producer prices, and direct emissions.

claims.text: Now record each intermediate invoice with both seller and buyer identified. During the reference year, S purchases 10 CU of electricity from F, 10 CU of electricity from G, and 20 CU of services from itself; F purchases 20 CU of services from S, and G purchases 30 CU of services from S. All other intermediate transactions are zero, and the remaining outputs go to final users—leaving 90 CU each for F and G and 30 CU for S. Preserving buyer and seller identities across these five intermediate invoices is what makes it possible to locate the exact same delivery in both process and economic accounts when testing for double counting.
claims.scope: Five annual intermediate transactions with explicit seller-to-buyer identities.

claims.text: Once generators F and G are aggregated into a single electricity sector E, individual invoice identities vanish from the sectoral table. The aggregated accounts report only 200 CU of output for E and 100 CU for S. With sellers in rows and buyers in columns, the use table records 20 CU/year of electricity sold to S, 50 CU/year of services sold to E, and 20 CU/year of services used internally by S. Dividing each column by the buyer's total output yields input coefficients of 0.25 CU of services per CU of E output, and 0.2 CU of electricity plus 0.2 CU of services per CU of S output. Direct CO₂ intensities are (40 + 120)/200 = 0.8 kg/CU for E and 30/100 = 0.3 kg/CU for S. When F is later separated out as a foreground process, this aggregated table still embeds F's output, purchases, sales, and emissions.
claims.scope: Aggregated sectoral accounts obtained by combining the two electricity generators into sector E.

claims.text: See what happens if F is linked to the unadjusted sectoral table. Counting F's direct emissions alone gives 8 kg CO₂ for 20 kWh, and the economic table appears to fill in F's upstream service inputs. From the invoices, F requires 0.2 CU of services per kWh generated, and S requires 0.1 kWh from F per CU of service output. Coupling both links without disaggregating sector E means producing 100 CU of services requires both the 20 CU of electricity already in E's column and the 10 kWh explicitly linked from F—a combined 30 CU at the uniform price, compared with only 20 CU on the invoices. The extra 10 CU is precisely F's sale of electricity to S, counted once inside sector E and a second time through the explicit process link.
claims.scope: Double counting caused by coupling a named generator directly to an unadjusted sectoral table.

claims.text: Eliminating that overlap requires removing F from the annual accounts before forming background coefficients. First subtract F's full base-year activity—100 CU of output and 40 kg CO₂—from sector E's totals, rather than deducting one-fifth for the 20 kWh wall demand; how much activity the final demand requires is determined only after the coefficients are built and solved. Next adjust both cross-boundary transactions by buyer and seller: in the use table, S's sales to E drop from 50 to 30 CU (leaving G's purchases), E's sales to S drop from 20 to 10 CU (leaving G's sales), and S's internal use of 20 CU stays intact. The residual electricity sector now consists solely of G, whose 100 CU output and 120 kg CO₂ give a recalculated intensity of 1.2 kg/CU; G requires 0.3 CU of services per CU, while S requires 0.1 CU of G's electricity and 0.2 CU of services per CU. The two removed transactions do not disappear—they move out of the background interior into the explicit cross-boundary linkages.
claims.scope: Disaggregating the foreground activity by transaction counterpart and recalculating residual background coefficients.

claims.text: With the accounts separated, each of the three suppliers receives its own supply–demand balance row. Let u denote F's total electricity generation (kWh), v the residual electricity sector G's output (CU), and w the service sector's output (CU). The three balances read u − 0.1w = 20, v − 0.1w = 0, and w − 0.2u − 0.3v − 0.2w = 0. The first row supplies S's demand for F's electricity and delivers the remaining 20 kWh to the wall; the second row scales G to supply S's remaining electricity demand, with the two 0.1 coefficients carrying units of kWh/CU and CU/CU, respectively; and the third row ensures that S supplies all services required by F, G, and itself.
claims.scope: Supply–demand balance equations across the three activity coordinates.

claims.text: Substituting the two electricity equations into the service balance yields 0.75w = 4, giving w = 16/3 CU, v = 8/15 CU, and u = 308/15 kWh. The excess generation by F above the 20 kWh final delivery supplies exactly the electricity needed by the service activities supporting that delivery. The resulting power-supply inventory is 0.4u + 1.2v + 0.3w = 784/75 kg CO₂, or approximately 10.453333 kg CO₂. Solving the unaggregated F, G, and S accounts directly yields the exact same activities and emissions, confirming that disaggregation preserves every supply relationship when transactions are known.
claims.scope: Positive activity solution and power-supply inventory when supplier identities are known.

claims.text: Returning to the unadjusted model shows why balanced equations cannot by themselves detect double counting. Its three rows become u − 0.1w = 20, v − 0.2w = 0, and w − 0.2u − 0.25v − 0.2w = 0, where u is F's generation (kWh), v is the aggregated electricity sector's output (CU) under raw average coefficients, and w is service output (CU). Here, F's electricity sale to S enters both the 0.1 link in the first row and the 0.2 coefficient in the second row. The system still balances cleanly at u = 1500/73, v = 80/73, and w = 400/73, yielding 0.4u + 0.8v + 0.3w = 784/73 kg CO₂—0.286393 kg higher than the disaggregated result. Equation balance therefore does not rule out double counting; only the invoices reveal the duplicated 10 CU delivery. Moreover, because the gap between the two full models also reflects altered average emission intensities and service recipes, that 0.286393 kg difference cannot be labeled simply as "one double-counted emission."
claims.scope: Demonstration that closed balance equations can coexist with duplicated underlying transactions.

claims.text: What if the invoices are lost—can an aggregated sectoral table recover who actually supplied whom? Construct an alternative invoice ledger with identical sectoral totals but different bilateral flows: S still buys 20 CU of electricity, now entirely from G, while F and G keep their annual generation, prices, direct emissions, and service purchases unchanged, shifting final-user residuals to 100 CU for F and 80 CU for G. Once aggregated into sector E, both ledgers produce identical total outputs, identical cell-by-cell inter-sector uses, and identical direct emissions. From the sectoral table alone, it is impossible to tell whether F supplied any electricity to S; the same aggregate totals accommodate distinct transaction networks.
claims.scope: Swapping the service sector's electricity supplier while holding all aggregated sectoral totals fixed.

claims.text: Under this second invoice ledger, F still buys services from S but no longer supplies electricity to S, so its balance reduces to u = 20 kWh for the wall, while G supplies all of S's electricity (v = 0.2w). Substituting into the service balance gives w = 200/37 CU and v = 40/37 CU, raising the power-supply inventory to 404/37 kg CO₂ (approximately 10.918919 kg). Applying the first ledger's result simply because the aggregated sectoral tables match underestimates emissions by 0.465586 kg. Holding the first ledger's activities fixed (including w = 16/3) and testing them in the second ledger's balance equations reveals a supply surplus of 8/15 kWh for F and a supply deficit of 8/15 CU for G—comparing supply–demand residuals for a single activity vector rather than differences between separately solved equilibria. At the uniform price of 1 CU/kWh, converting F's surplus into 8/15 CU makes the two residuals cancel out in the aggregated electricity row, even though the named supplier is wrong and the two generators carry different emission intensities. Consistency at the sectoral aggregate level therefore cannot substitute for evidence of supplier identity.
claims.scope: Inventory outcome for the same external delivery under an alternative bilateral supply network.

claims.text: Even when a process inventory lists product names, analysts may still not know which background items to subtract. Agez et al. illustrate this with a pump modeled at two levels of detail: a fine inventory separates direct stainless steel from steel embedded in purchased components, whereas a coarse inventory merges both into 1 kg of stainless steel. Under the authors' assumptions, the standalone process emissions stay unchanged, yet the coarse inventory hides which commodity categories the components originally belonged to—altering both which add-ons are linked and which overlaps are removed when matching by name.
claims.scope: Mismatch between physical process resolution and monetary commodity groups in the Agez et al. pump example.

claims.text: Pricing the pump exposes a further complication. Agez et al. assume a pump price of EUR 12 and a machinery-sector average steel purchase of EUR 0.03 per EUR of output, implying EUR 0.36 of steel per pump in the economic table, whereas the process side records 1 kg of steel valued at EUR 0.75/kg. Applying by-product correction (BPC) to subtract the covered monetary value yields 0.36 − 0.75 = −0.39 EUR per pump. The negative sign sits on the monetary add-on while the 1 kg of physical steel remains positive, signaling that the specific process's steel expenditure exceeds the sector average—and interpreting that gap still depends on how items were matched and priced.
claims.scope: Negative monetary add-on and its accounting meaning in the hypothetical pump example.
caveats: The negative value carries units of EUR per pump; all pump and steel prices and quantities belong to the authors' hypothetical illustration.

claims.text: Alternative correction rules still require identifying the same underlying activity. A binary rule sees that steel already appears in the process inventory and zeroes out the background steel add-on, yet steel embedded in aggregated components may remain inside a "fabricated metal products" add-on. Conversely, tier-wise purchase correction (TPC) traces high-contribution upstream paths to locate steel, which can lead to steel used in factory-building construction rather than the pump body. Although both flows are steel, whether subtraction is valid depends on end use, supply tier, and what the process model already covers.
claims.scope: Identification evidence required respectively by name-based zeroing and high-contribution path subtraction.

claims.text: Adding missing activities also requires checking accuracy against a known benchmark. Yang, Heijungs, and Brandão construct a small economy where every activity is known, then remove the maize process so that the 0.5 kg of maize required for 1 kg of popcorn lacks a process record. At USD 2/kg, the missing input is worth USD 1, which a tiered hybrid model supplies from an agricultural sector aggregating maize and wheat. Against the complete reference economy, the hybrid model's error magnitude is 65.3%, compared with 33.7% for the truncated process model; once the authors lower wheat's emission intensity so the two crops become more similar, the error ranking reverses. Exact prices and matching reference years are held constant throughout—what drives the reversal is whether the sector-average recipe represents the missing maize.
claims.scope: Trade-off between truncation error and aggregation error in the constructed economy of Yang, Heijungs, and Brandão (2017).
caveats: On page 240 of the source, expanded Equation (24) prints +1 for the agriculture/popcorn entry while Equation (25) prints −1, and page 239 text cites 2 kg for energy emissions where the matrix coefficient is 1.5. We report the authors' published error percentages rather than presenting a silently modified matrix as an exact reproduction.

claims.text: That counterexample defines conditions under which hybrid gap-filling worsens an estimate, leaving open how representative such conditions are in real economies. In an institutional author abstract responding to Yang et al., Pomponi and Lenzen report that altering technical linkages in the five-sector economy makes process truncation error larger than hybrid aggregation error, and support their representativeness claim by comparing dominant eigenvalues of the altered system with those of real economies. We can report those authors' conclusion here, but because the abstract does not provide the full matrices, error calculations, or real-economy eigenvalue comparisons, it does not allow an independent verification of empirical accuracy.
claims.scope: Constructed counterexample versus representativeness objection regarding real-world inter-industry linkages.
caveats: Based solely on the author abstract archived in the University of York Research Database; verifying item-by-item coefficients and recalculations for the alternative economy requires the full article.

The author abstract omits full model inputs, error derivations, and real-economy dominant-eigenvalue comparison data, and even a full matrix would not by itself substitute for an empirical representativeness test.

claims.text: At database scale, Jakobs, Schulte, and Pauliuk examine how price variance alters hybrid background additions. Mapping ecoinvent 3.5 processes to the 2012 EXIOBASE 3.6 economic table, they run 10,000 Monte Carlo draws using BACI international trade unit prices and proxy distributions to compare the binary rule with the similar technological attributes method (STAM), which screens upstream add-ons using technological relationships across product categories. While their conceptual framework retains Cᵈ and cites Suh's 2006 reply noting that downstream feedback is often small though potentially significant in some applications, the actual computation uses pyLCAIO and constructs only the upstream matrix Cᵘ. All quantitative results below must be interpreted within that implementation.
claims.scope: Experimental design of Jakobs, Schulte, and Pauliuk (2021) for testing price variance and upstream hybrid screening rules.
caveats: The characterization of Suh's 2006 reply relies on its named attribution on page 3 of Jakobs et al. (2021); the full text and examples of the original reply remain to be verified directly.

claims.text: Comparing percentage increases first requires inspecting the denominator. For a monthly Swiss household consumption basket (Tables 4–5 of Jakobs et al., 2021), row Γ includes only the 12,065 processes represented in ecoinvent, excluding activities modeled separately in EXIOBASE or AGRIBALYSE; that process baseline is 1,144 kg CO₂-eq (tabulated in units of 10² kg CO₂-eq). Under BACI trade unit prices and proxy distributions, median added IO footprints are 88 kg CO₂-eq under STAM and 163 kg CO₂-eq under the binary rule, corresponding to 7.7% and 14.3% of the Γ baseline. Restricting the denominator to row Λ—the 4,789 hybridized processes, with a process baseline of 513 kg CO₂-eq—leaves both absolute additions unchanged while raising their shares to 17.2% and 31.8%. Reporting percentage shifts without stating the baseline scope therefore obscures what is being compared.
claims.scope: Added IO footprint and process-baseline scope for the monthly Swiss household consumption basket.
caveats: Percentages follow the published table values and absolute totals are reported in kilograms; because tabulated columns are rounded, dividing displayed figures directly may differ in the last digit.

claims.text: Asking how much individual process intensities rise shifts the comparison object again. Across 6,264 hybridized processes, Jakobs et al. report median carbon-footprint intensity increases of 6.1% under STAM and 16.7% under the binary rule—metrics that must be kept distinct from the household consumption-basket shares. Moreover, their Monte Carlo analysis varies prices independently without simultaneously propagating uncertainty from sectoral aggregation, process supply-chain data, or characterization factors. Such results show how outputs respond under a specified database, mapping, screening rule, and price distribution, but assessing real-world error at a specific facility still requires independent benchmarks and site-level data.
claims.scope: Distinction between price-variance sensitivity and empirical footprint error benchmarks.

claims.text: Auditing a hybrid inventory therefore starts with a single traceable transaction. Verify seller, buyer, product, reference year, and valuation basis to locate the identical input or output on both sides; for electricity delivered in different time periods or at different voltage levels, also verify whether the same generation record applies. Once transaction identity is established, disaggregate the supply, use, and direct-emission accounts, recalculate coefficient denominators, and verify each supplier's solved activity. Whenever two distinct purchase patterns explain the same sectoral table yet yield different inventories, retain both interpretations until invoices or other procurement records resolve them.
claims.scope: Audit workflow from transaction identity and annual account disaggregation to balance verification and applicability judgment.

claims.text: Hybrid inventories can link known purchases to matching economic background data, while sectoral input structures can flag potentially omitted activities or approximate missing inputs. Even after the matrix equations balance, analysts must still verify who actually supplies the flow and whether sector-average recipes represent the missing process—and when comparing methods, preserve independent cases alongside counterexamples that challenge prior expectations. The section below places process-based and hybrid inventories side by side within mainstream standards and database frameworks to see how each governance regime sets its own comparability thresholds across cut-offs, capital goods, economic data admission, and double-counting control.
claims.scope: Diagnostic framework integrating formal solvability, data representativeness, and system coverage; not a general ranking of methods.
caveats: The two cited works share an author and cannot be treated as independent replication; their methodological discussion does not establish a general superiority ranking for real-world products or databases.

claims.text: All LCI standards and database frameworks confront the same structural dilemma: 100% of the true total inventory is never directly observable under any life cycle modeling approach. The European Commission's International Reference Life Cycle Data System (ILCD) Handbook (2010, §6.6.3) states explicitly that, regardless of modeling path, the 100% total must always be approximated by extrapolating from measured or calculated data. Process networks leave lightweight inputs, capital goods, and purchased services outside the matrix, creating truncation error; IO and hybrid inventories close upstream boundaries via macroeconomic accounts, but introduce sectoral aggregation, price conversion, and double-counting subtraction errors. Standards differ not because any claims to eliminate error, but because each chooses which error class to govern inside its boundary and which to exclude from permissible practice.
claims.scope: Cross-framework comparison of inventory completeness, anchored in ILCD Handbook (2010, §6.6.3) and Suh (2004) boundary truncation analysis.

claims.text: Even within purely process-based frameworks, four major public standards and guidelines diverge on cut-off thresholds, capital goods, and purchased services. The ILCD Handbook (2010, §§6.6.2–6.6.3) defines quantitative cut-offs by environmental-impact coverage (such as 85% or 95%) and includes capital goods plus purchased services—cleaning, legal, marketing, and office services—in principle unless proven insignificant. The European Union Product Environmental Footprint (PEF) method (Commission Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279, Annex I) forbids cut-offs during screening, caps cumulative cut-offs at 3.0% in full studies (jointly constraining mass, energy, and environmental significance), excludes capital goods by default, limits ILCD entry-level (ILCD-EL) proxy data to 10% of the single overall score, and requires verified exclusion when no compliant proxy exists. The Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Protocol Product Standard (2011, Chapter 7) classifies capital goods and corporate services such as R&D, administration, and marketing as optional non-attributable processes, allowing attributable processes to be excluded only when data are unavailable, no proxy exists, and estimates fall below disclosure thresholds. By contrast, ecoinvent v3 (2013) explicitly models capital goods by lifetime and capacity, declares no strict quantitative cut-off and no cut-off for recycled by-products, and fills data gaps using stoichiometry with a default 95% yield alongside mass and monetary balances.
claims.scope: Comparison of cut-off rules, capital goods, and service boundaries across four process-based standards and database guidelines.

claims.text: Whether environmentally extended input–output (EEIO) data may enter a product inventory marks the sharpest institutional divide between process standards and hybrid frameworks. Neither the ILCD Handbook (2010) nor EU PEF (2021) provides EEIO or hybrid gap-filling clauses: their data hierarchies stop at compliant process datasets and controlled proxies, preferring transparent exclusion over importing macroeconomic sector factors. Although ecoinvent v3 maintains unit-process monetary balances incorporating value added, its core structure remains a physical unit-process network. Among the four process frameworks, only the GHG Protocol Product Standard (§8.3.4 and Box 8.2) explicitly allows financial expenditure data multiplied by EEIO emission factors for screening and upstream estimation, while noting EEIO's broad coverage and coarse sectoral resolution. Mapped onto the three hybrid architectures above, attaching EEIO factors to expenditure records resembles tiered hybrid analysis rather than Suh's (2004) integrated hybrid framework with coupled physical and monetary accounts.
claims.scope: Institutional comparison of EEIO data admission in process standards versus tiered and integrated hybrid architectures.

claims.text: Once process data and macroeconomic accounts coexist, double-counting governance must change accordingly. In process-centered frameworks such as the GHG Protocol Product Standard (§8.3.4), avoiding overlap relies primarily on compilers manually checking which upstream processes each emission factor already covers so that metered fuel or electricity is not counted again inside a spend-based factor. In systematic hybrid LCI, however, process networks and sectoral IO tables overlap across multiple supply tiers, requiring explicit matrix-subtraction or screening algorithms—such as Suh's (2004) pre-subtraction of process-covered transactions from supply, use, and environmental accounts, or the binary correction, BPC, TPC, and STAM procedures compared by Agez et al. (2019/2020). As the three-supplier invoice ledger demonstrated, aggregate sectoral totals alone cannot reveal which generator supplied the service sector's electricity; any rule operating solely on sector totals therefore remains an assumption-bound approximation rather than a substitute for verifying specific supply relationships.
claims.scope: Comparison between manual scope checking in process standards and algorithmic double-counting subtraction in hybrid LCI.

claims.text: Comparing hybrid and process-based inventories across frameworks also requires harmonizing monetary conversion, sectoral aggregation, and denominator definitions. Whereas pure process inventories are bounded mainly by truncation depth and background-database coverage, hybrid inventories trade reduced truncation for three sensitivity switches absent from process standards: first, aggregation error when sectoral homogeneity fails (illustrated by Yang et al.'s 2017 popcorn counterexample, while Pomponi and Lenzen's 2018 response underscores that relative error depends on economic structure); second, conversion uncertainty from producer versus purchaser prices and unit-price dispersion; and third, denominator choice—as Jakobs et al. (2021) show, normalizing against all relevant basket processes (Γ) versus only the hybridized subset (Λ) shifts percentage-increase judgments for the same database. In addition, ecoinvent v3 (§6.4) captures physical causal links without direct monetary payment, whereas EEIO transmits upstream burdens strictly along monetary transactions, leaving their coverage of unpriced public services misaligned.
claims.scope: Effects of monetary-to-physical conversion, sectoral aggregation, denominator scope, and unpriced physical causality on cross-framework comparability.

claims.text: The comparison table above establishes no universal ranking—neither that hybrid inventories always outperform process standards nor that a strict 3.0% cut-off is inherently more reliable—but rather the conditions under which each boundary regime holds. For the same product system, if one study follows EU PEF rules (excluding capital goods by default with a 3.0% cut-off), a second uses ecoinvent v3 with modeled infrastructure, and a third overlays EEIO add-ons for purchased services and capital goods, differences among their totals confound expanded boundary coverage with sectoral aggregation, price conversion, and subtraction assumptions. Without first aligning boundary declarations, capital-good and service lists, price bases, double-counting rules, and denominators, comparing raw process and hybrid totals cannot support a robust methodological preference; whether aggregation error or truncation error dominates remains an empirical question governed by sectoral resolution and price dispersion. Having examined service references, process networks, and hybrid inventories, the next part turns to the supply side: how burdens are partitioned when one process yields multiple products, and which supplying activities respond when demand changes.
claims.scope: Epistemic boundaries and explicit unknowns in cross-framework inventory comparisons.
caveats: This comparison synthesizes published standards and hybrid-LCI literature and does not substitute for empirical testing of sectoral resolution and price distributions in a specific industry.

claims.text: When a single process delivers multiple products, its emissions occur jointly rather than separately for each output. Recording an inventory for each individual product requires deciding how to divide those shared emissions. Evaluating a switch to an alternative supply route, by contrast, can compare two systems constructed to deliver the same set of functions. Ekvall and Tillman (1997) reserve "allocation" for the first operation—proportional partitioning—and use "allocation procedure" for the broader set of methods that also includes avoiding partitioning through system expansion. Whenever a study invokes an allocation procedure, the first check is whether it is partitioning an existing account or assembling comparable sets of activities.
claims.scope: Terminological hierarchy in Ekvall and Tillman (1997)
caveats: Preserves the authors' terminological scope without treating their definitions as universal across all literature.

claims.text: Choosing an approach depends on what information the study aims to provide. Ekvall, Tillman, and Molander (2005) distinguish "retrospective life cycle assessment (LCA)," which describes environmentally relevant flows within a system and its subsystems, from "prospective LCA," which describes how a potential decision changes those flows. The distinction tracks the question being asked: a study may examine the consequences of a past decision or describe a system not yet operating. Both asking which burdens are associated with a product and asking how an action increases or decreases burdens can inform decisions. The normative ethical rationale supporting either question must be stated explicitly rather than inferred from the label alone.
claims.scope: Information goals and normative ethics framework in Ekvall, Tillman, and Molander (2005)
caveats: Retains the authors' original labels without unconditionally mapping them onto all contemporary attributional or consequential LCA definitions.

claims.text: Appealing to "causality" requires specifying which causal direction is being traced. Ekvall and Tillman (1997) separate two questions: what causes production to occur, and what consequences follow when production changes. Expected sales revenue can help explain why a process operates, whereas a change in recycled-material supply requires examining whether other production activities are affected. The authors argue that advising a decision that alters material flows requires tracing the consequences of that choice—a requirement tied specifically to flows affected by the decision and its intended purpose. Switching a raw material, for instance, does not necessarily alter packaging recycling even when both belong to the same product system.
claims.scope: Causal directions and decision-affected material flows in Ekvall and Tillman (1997, §§3–5.1)
caveats: The revenue example illustrates how the paper interprets other claims rather than providing independent proof of the cited primary works.

claims.text: A study must also specify which burdens are treated as shared. Viewed at the level of an individual recycling process, the operation simultaneously treats upstream waste and supplies downstream material, raising the question of how to partition that single process. Following the same material across successive uses brings primary production and final disposal into the shared account as well. Ekvall and Tillman (1997) distinguish three levels: an individual process, a single product life cycle, and a material cascade across consecutive uses. Even identical allocation percentages assign different burdens to a product if one applies to a single process and the other applies to an entire material cascade.
claims.scope: Problem framing across open-loop material cascade levels in Ekvall and Tillman (1997)
caveats: The three levels reflect the framing of that paper and do not require every recycling study to adopt the same hierarchy.

claims.text: System expansion aligns two routes so that both deliver the same set of functions. Frischknecht (1998) shows that one may either add the missing function to a single-product route or subtract a reference supply of that function from the joint route. Ekvall and Tillman (1997) frame the technosphere as holding demand for all other functions constant while tracing the affected processes—a simplification of the broader socioeconomic system. Identifying which supplier actually expands or withdraws depends on functional performance, demand, and downstream activities; it cannot be read off an addition or subtraction sign.
claims.scope: Function-matched comparison structures and whole-system assumptions
caveats: Formal algebraic operations do not prove actual market displacement, nor do all boundary expansions represent causal substitution.

claims.text: When a joint process delivers products X and Y in fixed proportions, output of X cannot be increased while holding Y constant. Frischknecht (1998) first separates processes that possess genuine physical causality suitable for partitioning from fixed-proportion joint production. Partitioning by mass, volume, or energy establishes a proportional convention rather than a description of how inputs respond when one output changes. Even describing an existing system may require asking what consequences follow from shutting down an operating process. Selecting an allocation procedure therefore depends on which relationships physically exist and which decision the study is meant to support.
claims.scope: Fixed-proportion joint production argument in Frischknecht (1998, §§7.4.1–7.4.2)
caveats: Reflects Frischknecht's 1998 dissertation rather than a separately verified Heijungs–Frischknecht co-authored theorem or a general mathematical result for variable joint production.

claims.text: The sections that follow apply two distinct calculations to the same hypothetical batch of co-products. First, production is held fixed to compute each product's share of emissions; summing the two shares must recover the original batch total. Second, the two delivered services are held fixed while the supplying activities are changed, requiring both routes to deliver the full set of services. The chapter then examines which questions each calculation can answer and how a chosen rule must be justified. Applying route differences to an actual decision still requires evidence showing how supply will respond.
claims.scope: Three-layer analytical framework: burden partitioning, activity change, and rule justification
caveats: This three-question structure is an analytical organizing framework rather than a verbatim requirement of an external standard.

claims.text: Begin by holding production constant. Suppose a joint batch process J delivers a fixed output of 4 kg of X and 6 kg of Y, whose quantities cannot be varied independently. X and Y represent distinct material services, each meeting specified grade, location, and time-period requirements; sharing the kilogram unit does not make them interchangeable. All products, quantities, prices, emissions, utilization scenarios, and supply responses in this teaching case are stipulated by the author, while carbon dioxide (CO₂) and sulfur dioxide (SO₂) retain their chemical identities. First, without changing any production, how should this batch inventory be attributed to X and Y? Next, holding the same pair of services constant, how does the inventory change under an alternative supply route? Both questions use the same numbers, yet they do not form the same study.
claims.scope: Hypothetical fixed-proportion joint batch: separating product-share attribution from service-supply comparison

claims.text: The inventory is recorded across four distinct operations, each with its own reference basis. One unit of J is the entire joint batch; one unit of S-X or S-Y supplies 1 kg of a material functionally equivalent to X or Y, respectively; and one unit of W-Y treats 1 kg of unused joint Y without material or energy recovery. In every ordered pair below, the first entry is fossil CO₂ emitted to air (in kg) and the second is SO₂ emitted to air (in g): J = (10, 20), S-X = (5, 1), S-Y = (3, 4), and W-Y = (0.5, 0.2). Quantities may be added only within the same elementary-flow row; no characterization factors are applied, and CO₂ mass is not labeled CO₂-equivalent.
claims.scope: Reference bases, elementary-flow identities, and units for the four operations in the hypothetical case

claims.text: Before calculating, fix the accounting boundary. All listed emissions from J constitute a joint burden, with no separate single-product sub-activities. Each of the remaining three operations contributes its listed inventory and is assumed not to overlap with J. Unlisted activities and emissions lie outside the model's coverage and must not be treated as physically zero. This setup compares operation over a bounded period without modeling plant construction, changes in existing capital stock, capacity constraints, price feedback, or secondary market chains. The example therefore tests how explicitly specified inputs are partitioned and compared; exhausting the listed inventory does not turn the case into a full life cycle or a complete elemental mass balance.
claims.scope: Operational boundary, joint-burden scope, and non-overlap assumptions of the hypothetical case

claims.text: First partition the batch by mass, assuming both X and Y are fully used and sold. Under this author-specified mass rule, X takes 4 ÷ (4 + 6) = 2/5 of the joint burden and Y takes 3/5. Multiplying each row by these shares assigns (4, 8) to X and (6, 12) to Y, which sum back to J's (10, 20). Dividing by each product's mass yields (1, 2) per kg of X and (1, 2) per kg of Y, expressed in kg CO₂/kg product and g SO₂/kg product. Identical per-kilogram figures are an artifact of the chosen mass ratio and do not imply that the two services are equivalent.
claims.scope: Mass-based allocation shares and row-by-row inventory partitioning when the entire batch is utilized

claims.text: Next partition the same unchanged production and emissions by sales revenue. Stipulate prices of 3 currency units (CU)/kg for X and 1 CU/kg for Y, where CU is a teaching monetary unit; batch revenues are 12 CU and 6 CU, totaling 18 CU. X and Y then receive shares of 2/3 and 1/3, giving batch inventories of (20/3, 40/3) for X and (10/3, 20/3) for Y, whose sum remains (10, 20). Per kilogram, X carries (5/3, 10/3) and Y carries (5/9, 10/9). Only the partitioning criterion changed; the technologies and physical emissions of all four operations remained untouched.
claims.scope: Revenue-based allocation shares and row-by-row inventory partitioning under stipulated prices

claims.text: Summing the shares assigned to X and Y verifies that the batch emissions have been fully accounted for. Both mass and revenue rules produce non-negative, determinate shares that add back to the total. That shared property checks for omissions or double counting, but it cannot decide between mass and revenue. Mass expresses a uniform quantity convention, while revenue links attribution to sales value; either choice still requires explaining why that form of attribution fits the study's purpose. Raising X's price alters its revenue share without enabling J to produce more X independently, and dividing by kilograms merely changes the display denominator. Ledger additivity, product function, and production response are already three distinct things to check.
claims.scope: Accounting properties of additive shares and their inability to settle rule selection

claims.text: Selecting a partitioning rule also invites asking who is making the decision. Frischknecht (1998) distinguishes an individual price-taking competitor from multiple decision-makers who form a voluntary coalition to negotiate joint gains; where decision-makers can set integrated prices incorporating environmental factors, he formulates the problem as joint price-and-output optimization. In the first case, a "perfect market" means firms take prices as given, not that market prices internalize environmental externalities. The second case requires voluntary participation by all parties. Each setting calls for examining demand, alternative supply, or coalition conditions rather than choosing an attribution rule simply because several firms appear in the same table.
claims.scope: Decision-maker and market classification in Frischknecht (1998, pp. 104–106)
caveats: This taxonomy is the author's proposal; summarizing it does not independently verify the full optimization, game-theoretic, or disutility derivations.

claims.text: Ekvall, Tillman, and Molander (2005, §3.1) offer a specific rationale for revenue allocation: if the particular task of a retrospective LCA is to describe the causes of environmental burdens, allocating a multi-output process by the economic value of its outputs is reasonable. Without that specific purpose, they argue, an objective basis for choosing an allocation method is hard to establish. That rationale applies to the stated attribution task; selling prices alone still do not tell an analyst which supplier will cut output if procurement increases.
claims.scope: Economic-value allocation rationale in Ekvall, Tillman, and Molander (2005, §3.1, p. 1229)
caveats: The authors' "retrospective" label is not automatically identical to all modern attributional or consequential definitions, and their argument is not a binding reporting standard.

claims.text: In the closing passage of §7.5.4 (p. 119), Frischknecht (1998) asks how a joint product should be compared with external competitors. Sales-value allocation distributes joint burdens according to each product's "ability to bear" them. Yet when allocated shares are used to compare a joint product against competing products, the comparison must satisfy his criterion of environmental and economic competitiveness. To test that criterion, he recommends incorporating environmental information about competing products, assuming firms and customers evaluate it through a disutility function. Ordinary market prices omit part of the information such a comparison requires—a judgment bounded to the competitive setting he analyzes.
claims.scope: Sales-value criterion for external product comparison in Frischknecht (1998, §7.5.4, p. 119)
caveats: This passage does not substitute for full verification of the disutility-function or competitiveness derivations, nor does it establish a universal allocation hierarchy.

claims.text: The two cited passages address different evaluative purposes: Ekvall, Tillman, and Molander (2005, §3.1) ask how to describe the causes of burdens, whereas Frischknecht (1998, §7.5.4) asks how to compare a joint product against external competitors. Revenue-based partitioning can be defensible for the first question while still lacking competitor information needed for the second. Placing these two arguments side by side is an editorial comparison here; no evidence shows the two sets of authors directly debated those specific passages. Returning to batch J, recording an existing batch requires stating the chosen partitioning rule, whereas evaluating a switch in supply requires listing the activities that actually change.
claims.scope: Contrasting evaluative goals of two cited primary arguments and mapping them to the hypothetical batch

claims.text: Now allow production activities to change while keeping delivered services fixed at 4 kg of X and 6 kg of Y at the specified delivery point and period. Begin with the full-use premise: all joint Y meets existing demand for Y with a one-to-one match in quality, location, timing, and downstream use; joint supply actually displaces the listed separate supply; S-Y can withdraw by the matching quantity; and no extra intermediate treatment is needed. Every one of these conditions is explicitly stipulated in the problem. Selling a product or sharing a similar function does not prove them on its own; only together with these conditions does the route difference below represent the stipulated supply response.
claims.scope: Fixed service basket under full utilization and feasible withdrawal of separate supply

claims.text: Write both alternatives as positive activity routes. Without J, the fixed service basket is supplied by 4 units of S-X and 6 units of S-Y, emitting 4 × 5 + 6 × 3 = 38 kg of CO₂ and 4 × 1 + 6 × 4 = 28 g of SO₂, or (38, 28). With the joint route, 1 unit of J supplies both services with emissions of (10, 20). Both routes deliver the required X and Y, and every process emits positive quantities. Subtracting the separate route from the joint route gives a net difference of (−28, −8): under the stated conditions, both elementary flows decline without invoking any negative physical production activity.
claims.scope: Full-utilization scenario: two positive routes delivering the same service basket and their row-by-row difference

claims.text: To isolate the reference supply of Y, rearrange the full route difference algebraically as J − (4S-X + 6S-Y) = (J − 6S-Y) − 4S-X. Define the bracketed term as the comparison residual anchored on X: R_X = J − 6S-Y = (−8, −4). Because the reference supply of Y has been factored out, R_X represents the quantity to be compared against 4 units of S-X, anchored to the 4 kg batch of X—or (−2, −1) per kg of X. Subtracting 4S-X from R_X recovers the exact route difference (−28, −8). Subtracting Y's reference supply thus has a transparent origin: both routes had to deliver the Y service, and algebra merely groups one part of the full comparison inside parentheses.
claims.scope: Full-utilization scenario: algebraic derivation of the X-anchored comparison residual

claims.text: Whenever a residual is negative, check what was subtracted from which emission. Process J still emits 10 kg of CO₂ and 20 g of SO₂; it does not remove either gas from the atmosphere. The negative residual arises solely from deducting the specified S-Y reference supply, so its value depends on the Y service and the chosen reference technology. For comparing two functionally matched routes, the algebraic identity already holds. Interpreting that difference as an actual market change, however, requires evidence that S-Y supply genuinely decreases and how suppliers respond. Here that response is stipulated as a premise; subtraction cannot prove the response itself, nor is the residual an intrinsic property of X detached from this context.
claims.scope: Reference dependence and supply-response conditions behind a negative residual

claims.text: Placing three per-kilogram numbers side by side tests whether a shared denominator makes them interchangeable. For CO₂ per kg of X, mass allocation yields 1, revenue allocation yields 5/3, and the comparison residual yields −2, all in kg CO₂/kg X. The common unit does not erase the difference in questions: the first two partition a shared batch inventory by convention, whereas the third carries Y's reference supply into a route comparison. SO₂ makes the contrast sharper: mass allocation assigns 2 g of SO₂ per kg of X—higher than S-X's 1 g—yet comparing the complete service basket shows the joint route saves 8 g of SO₂ overall. Per-kilogram labels cannot be read directly as procurement conclusions for the whole service basket; purpose, denominator, and reference must travel with the number.
claims.scope: Distinguishing product shares, per-kilogram displays, and full service-basket comparisons

claims.text: What happens if one also anchors a residual on Y and then adds the two residuals together? Defining R_Y = J − 4S-X gives (−10, 16) for the 6 kg batch of Y. Adding R_X and R_Y as if they were a pair of product tags produces (−18, 12) rather than J's actual inventory of (10, 20). The missing (28, 8) is precisely the total basket saving: in two separate comparisons, X and Y each claimed the entire saving once. Two individually valid comparisons cannot be merged directly into additive attribution accounts; databases and reporting systems still require consistent system-level conventions.
claims.scope: Double-counting of system savings when residuals from different anchors are summed

claims.text: Next test how the fixed service basket is met when not all joint Y reaches its intended use. Suppose only a fraction q of joint Y reaches the specified service within the period, with each utilized kilogram still displacing 1 kg of S-Y under the original premises; the unused remainder goes to W-Y, and S-Y covers the service shortfall. Here q is an author-stipulated utilization scenario, not a probability or an arbitrary credit discount factor. Setting q = 1/2 means 3 kg of joint Y fulfill the service, 3 kg enter unrecovered waste treatment, and 3 kg of S-Y are purchased to fill the gap. Selling a co-product still does not automatically prove displacement, so the utilization and supply-reduction conditions remain in force.
claims.scope: Half-utilization scenario: utilization, waste treatment, and make-up supply under a fixed service basket

claims.text: Recording each physical destination yields a positive half-utilization route of 1J + 3S-Y + 3W-Y (with S-X = 0), rather than simply halving J's emissions or the entire route. Two quantity checks verify consistency: on the service ledger, 3 kg of utilized joint Y plus 3 kg of make-up S-Y deliver the required 6 kg of Y; on the output-fate ledger, 3 kg of utilized Y plus 3 kg sent to W-Y account for all 6 kg produced by J. Meanwhile X remains at 4 kg. These checks balance delivered services and batch output fates; without full material inputs, they do not establish a complete elemental mass balance.
claims.scope: Quantity checks on delivered services and joint-output fates in the half-utilization scenario

claims.text: Once services and output fates balance, compute the inventory. The half-utilization joint route sums J's (10, 20), make-up supply 3S-Y = (9, 12), and waste treatment 3W-Y = (3/2, 3/5), totaling (41/2, 163/5). Subtracting the unchanged separate route (38, 28)—in kg CO₂ and g SO₂—yields (−35/2, 23/5). CO₂ still declines, but SO₂ now rises; the full-utilization finding that both emissions fall no longer carries over. Because no impact characterization is applied, changes in two different units cannot be combined into an overall environmental ranking.
claims.scope: Row-by-row inventory and opposing emission changes in the half-utilization scenario

claims.text: Rearranging the difference shows exactly where make-up supply cancels out of the algebra. For a general utilization fraction q, the positive joint route is J + 6(1 − q)S-Y + 6(1 − q)W-Y. Subtracting the reference Y supply 6S-Y yields the residual R_X(q) = J + 6(1 − q)W-Y − 6q S-Y. At q = 1/2, this becomes J + 3W-Y − 3S-Y = (5/2, 43/5); subtracting 4S-X returns (−35/2, 23/5). Make-up supply is physically present in the positive route and cancels against the reference term only in the reduced expression. Noting that a simplified residual contains no positive make-up term is entirely different from claiming that no make-up supply occurred.
claims.scope: Algebraic cancellation between physical make-up supply and reference supply across utilization fractions

claims.text: Another layer of rationale for partitioning comes from how analysts interpret responsibility. Ekvall and Tillman (1997, §7) examine eight fairness perspectives on who should bear the burdens of primary production, recycling, and final disposal. Viewing the product that extracts a material as responsible for its eventual disposal pulls burdens toward the extraction end, whereas viewing the product that removes material from the technosphere as obliging replacement pulls burdens toward the disposal end. Physical processes never move; only the accounting target shifts. Formulas make such choices visible, but readers still need the justification for adopting a given notion of responsibility.
claims.scope: Fairness perspectives on burden responsibility in Ekvall and Tillman (1997, §7)
caveats: Does not propose newly verified equations or endorse any single fairness viewpoint as universally correct.
An erratum exists for the paper (DOI 10.1007/BF02978499); this discussion relies only on the textual fairness premises and does not use original Equations 16–18.

claims.text: Ekvall and Tillman (1997) also ask how an allocation procedure gains user acceptance and remains practicable. They explicitly warn against cherry-picking methods to confirm preconceived conclusions. Data availability, time, and implementation difficulty limit how far consequences can be traced, and the authors find no single procedure that satisfies every criterion simultaneously. Whenever a study simplifies for feasibility, it should state which relationships were omitted, which conclusions could be affected, and why the simplification is acceptable for the stated purpose.
claims.scope: Acceptability, feasibility, and methodological trade-offs in Ekvall and Tillman (1997)
caveats: These methodological discussions do not represent an empirical benchmark of all procedures, nor does expert consensus constitute sufficient scientific proof.

claims.text: Tracing the consequences of an action faces its own evidentiary and resource limits. Ekvall, Tillman, and Molander (2005) point out that a study cannot automatically capture every causal link, marginal technologies can be misidentified, and available resources bound how far the analysis can reach. Conversely, recording only existing burdens can miss changes triggered by a decision. In some applications, the two approaches complement each other. Before combining them, an analyst must state the information sought and the normative rationale for each, then judge which step of the decision each can legitimately support.
claims.scope: Mutual critiques and complementarity of retrospective and prospective approaches in Ekvall et al. (2005, §§4–5)
caveats: The hotel example in the paper is an illustrative argument rather than proof that all real-world actors behave as assumed.

claims.text: Ekvall, Tillman, and Molander (2005) use the Thorskog Castle conference hotel to ask whether an assessment method can itself alter behavior. The hotel operates a grid-connected small hydropower plant. If using one additional kilowatt-hour simply reduces grid exports by one kilowatt-hour, examining only the hotel's own generation inventory omits how the grid replaces that electricity. The authors further hypothesize that if such consequential scoring became widespread, the hotel might earn a more favorable score by disconnecting from the grid—even though surplus electricity that could have been exported would go unused. The example models conditional dependence on external supply and operator choices rather than an observed disconnection, reminding analysts to check the incentives an assessment rule creates.
claims.scope: Information differences and hypothetical behavioral incentives in the Thorskog Castle hotel scenario (Ekvall, Tillman, and Molander 2005)
caveats: This is an illustrative scenario built on supply and operator-response assumptions; it does not report an actual grid disconnection, current electricity factors, or empirical findings for all scoring regimes.

claims.text: Once a study adopts a named procedure, it must verify the exact version in force. Weidema's addendum dated August 25, 2001 removes the standalone requirement in old Rule 2 that a dependent co-product must actually substitute another product, rewrites Rules 2 and 3, and deletes Rule 4. It instructs readers to discard specified tables, figures, and Examples 10 and 11, explicitly noting that Example 10's conclusion is incorrect. Revisions alter branching logic and the conditions under which examples apply; running an outdated branch while citing the addendum does not bring old results into compliance. The addendum documents what changed, while the original article must still be consulted for full definitions and algorithms.
claims.scope: Revision instructions in Weidema's August 25, 2001 addendum
caveats: Documents only the addendum's revision instructions without inferring the numerical structure or recalculated results of the original examples.

claims.text: Under revised Rule 1, Weidema's addendum assigns 100% of the joint process and its exchanges to A, termed the "determining co-product," without restating in those two pages how A is identified or B defined. Subsequent rules track "intermediate treatment" separately. If the dependent co-product is fully utilized in other processes, Rule 2 assigns intermediate treatment to A and credits A with the avoided burden of the displaced process—plus any downstream life cycle changes caused by differences between the co-product and the displaced product. If it is not fully utilized, Rule 3 assigns intermediate treatment to B and credits B with the avoided waste-treatment burden of the co-product. Credits represent process burdens rather than sales revenue. Here A, B, and intermediate treatment are defined by Weidema's named rules and cannot be equated directly to this chapter's X, Y, and W-Y; removing one earlier branch test still leaves the displaced process and its conditions to be specified.
claims.scope: Scope and semantics of the revised rules in Weidema's 2001 addendum
caveats: Presents a conditional reading of the addendum rather than a universal rule for system expansion or a current ISO requirement.

claims.text: Both the half-utilization route above and Weidema's addendum contain subtracted terms, making it useful to contrast their premises. The worked case here defines two routes delivering the same service basket, lists unused-Y treatment and S-Y make-up supply explicitly, and then rearranges the route difference without invoking a determining-co-product rule. Weidema's addendum rewrites branching and attribution under its own definitions of determining co-products and intermediate treatment. Sharing a minus sign does not make the two problem formulations interchangeable. Applying any named procedure requires reading its original definitions, revisions, and example boundaries together rather than borrowing a familiar-looking equation.
claims.scope: Boundary between the hypothetical fixed-service-basket route and Weidema's revised procedure

claims.text: The label "system expansion" alone does not reveal which quantity a study will report. The International Reference Life Cycle Data System (ILCD) Handbook (2010, §6.5.3) encompasses both adding missing functions to make systems comparable and subtracting substituted supply to isolate a single-function inventory. The first compares complete functional bundles; the second must state which product's inventory remains and which supply was deducted. The handbook also cautions that algebraic correspondence does not guarantee identical meaning or interpretation. Given the same reference supply, a full route difference can be rearranged as the difference between the retained function's residual and its separate reference inventory, yielding the exact same net difference—yet the residual itself is not the full route difference, and moving terms across an equation does not prove that the deducted supply will actually decrease.
claims.scope: Two uses of system expansion in ILCD (2010) and distinct evidentiary roles in the fixed-reference derivation

claims.text: The European Union (EU) Product Environmental Footprint (PEF) general multifunctionality rules (Commission Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279, corrigendum OJ L 144, Annex I §4.5) specify the reporting object even more tightly. Step 1 requires testing subdivision or system expansion first; when system expansion is used, the co-product's additional function must be included and results reported for the expanded system as a whole rather than for a single co-product. Where functions, boundaries, and study conditions align, ILCD's function-addition approach and PEF Step 1 system expansion share the same reporting object. If applicable rules permit expanding the system to compare identical functional bundles, an analyst cannot declare expansion infeasible merely out of a preference to report a single product. Formal PEF product comparisons further require compliance with the relevant Product Environmental Footprint Category Rules (PEFCR); a matched service-basket example by itself does not confer that status.
claims.scope: Step 1 reporting object and comparison eligibility in EU PEF (2021/2279, corrigendum OJ L 144)
caveats: Compares general multifunctionality provisions; sector-specific rules for electricity, transport, recycling, energy recovery, and other domains must be checked separately.

claims.text: Once a function is selected for subtraction, the analyst must choose an inventory to represent it. Under ILCD (2010) micro-level decision support (Situation A, §6.5.4 Provisions I.a.ii–iv and vi), when subdivision and virtual subdivision are unavailable and general multifunctionality conditions hold, non-required dependent co-functions are substituted where possible by the average market consumption mix of functionally equivalent alternatives of sufficient scale. That mix normally excludes the studied co-function supply route itself; the full market mix may be retained only if both exception criteria hold—its environmental impact contribution is small and retaining it will not materially alter results. The handbook explicitly frames this as a pragmatic simplification of full consequential modeling: it selects a conditional average proxy without claiming to identify which individual firms cut output.
claims.scope: Average consumption-mix proxy and conditions under ILCD (2010) Situation A general material multifunctionality
caveats: Does not cover short-term marginal rules for inter-system links (I.a.iii) or waste and other ILCD situations.
Determining co-functions may not be credited under this dependent co-function branch; identity cannot be assigned by mass share or arbitrary naming.

claims.text: ILCD also defines "sufficient scale" concretely. Footnote 58 checks whether the annual quantity of the co-function supplied by the studied process does not exceed the annual production capacity replaced each year by the alternative supply. The test looks neither at total annual market sales alone nor at total installed capacity alone. Even in a large market, slow capital turnover can fail this criterion; likewise, scaling a study from one small producer to an entire industry changes the volume that must be absorbed. Meeting this handbook criterion and observing an actual firm reduce output are therefore two distinct forms of evidence.
claims.scope: Annual capacity-replacement scale criterion in ILCD footnote 58 and logical counterexamples
caveats: Explains the handbook's stated decision convention without claiming independent empirical validation in any specific market.

claims.text: Direct substitution under PEF Step 2 demands a different set of proofs—and may be entered only after subdivision and system expansion have been ruled out. PEF lists direct substitution as one route for resolving multifunctionality via relevant physical relationships, imposing two independent requirements simultaneously: empirical evidence demonstrating a direct substitution effect, and the ability to model the substituted product using a directly representative inventory. Matching product specifications, available volumes, and market shares cannot prove direct substitution by themselves; conversely, even when the displaced supplier is identified, applying an unrepresentative process or regional average dataset does not automatically satisfy the second requirement.
