A lower average in the bottom group therefore guarantees neither the ranking of an arbitrary pair of hours nor the exact kilograms of CO₂ saved by a specific load shift.
claims.scope: Bottom-decile grouping in the original study versus arbitrary hour-pair or magnitude inference
caveats: Error bars in Figure 2 represent 95% confidence intervals and parenthetical values in Table 1 represent standard deviations; the table caption's kgCO₂/MW and the figure axis and text unit kgCO₂/MWh are preserved as published without using Table 1 values in the finite-shift calculation below.
The time-period groups are defined separately by each signal rather than sharing a single implemented dispatch window across all signals.

This discussion follows the source paper's 10th-percentile threshold; without the raw time series or grouping code, tie-handling at the threshold is unverified and the low group is not assumed to contain exactly 10% of observations.

claims.text: Testing emission-rate magnitudes reveals a further distinction. Across quantile curves in the study's largest node group, dispatch and statistical models tracked both the ordering and magnitude of the benchmark more closely, though they still exhibited downward bias at the low end and upward bias at the high end, respectively. By contrast, the average emission signal did not separate a favorable low-response group as clearly as the other signals. Helping screen low-response hours, matching benchmark rate magnitudes, and accurately predicting the emission change of a concrete schedule are progressively stricter requirements; success at one level does not guarantee performance at the next.
claims.scope: Distinct performance of named signals in low-group screening versus rate-magnitude comparison in the largest node group
caveats: This does not claim that average-signal estimates are zero across all subregions or that all confidence intervals span zero, nor does it invalidate average signals for attributional accounting.

claims.text: Nilges and colleagues examine the problem from the dispatch-model side: over how large a demand change does a marginal emission rate computed around a given state remain valid? In a linear dispatch model with fixed costs, capacities, and emission factors, they identify a cost-optimal dispatch solution—specifying which units remain free to adjust and which units or transmission lines are binding—and determine how far demand can move before that optimal basis changes. Within that guaranteed validity range, the finite emission difference of the selected dispatch solution equals the marginal rate times the load change. Moving beyond that range means only that the guarantee no longer holds; it does not automatically imply that the emission rate changes, let alone that the net difference reverses sign. The allowable load-increase and load-decrease bounds reported in the paper belong to specific nodes, hours, and directions in that model rather than serving as universal grid thresholds.
claims.scope: Conditional guarantee of a selected linear dispatch basis and its non-necessity
caveats: This paragraph applies to a fixed selected optimal dispatch or emission-determined optimum; tied cost optima, degeneracy, and one-sided derivatives require explicit selection, because equal cost does not guarantee equal emissions.
Citations rely on visible equations and published text excerpts from the journal article record; the original SecMOD model was not executed and the raw publisher PDF bytes were not archived.

claims.text: Nilges and colleagues report validity ranges for perturbing one demand coordinate at a time. Applying that concept to a load shift requires checking a complete signed perturbation containing both a decrease and an increase. When the two endpoints are independent and each stays within its valid direction and bound, the two baseline rates can be combined directly; even in a coupled model, those rates still hold if the same linear response relationship generating both baseline rates remains intact along the entire joint path. Otherwise, the two complete schedules must be compared directly rather than mechanically stitching together two single-coordinate intervals. A lossy battery, for instance, must specify actual charging and discharging energies, power trajectories, and a shared initial and final state of charge rather than assuming an equal-energy shift; likewise, if validity bounds are defined in MW, specifying only total shifted MWh is insufficient.
claims.scope: Authorial conditional derivation from single-coordinate validity ranges to two-sided demand shifts
caveats: This does not claim that all hours in the original paper's implementation are independent or that the paper tested complete battery charge-discharge schedules.
Simultaneous shifts across multiple nodes also involve shared network constraints; the two-window example below deliberately excludes such coupling.

If multiple response branches meet at the baseline, two single-direction rates may belong to different branches; observing that the joint shift is also linear does not by itself prove those rates can be summed.

claims.text: A stylized author-constructed task isolates how shift magnitude alters the outcome. Consider 10 divisible jobs, each consuming 1 MWh in either window with identical equipment efficiency and output quality, all permitted to finish by the end of the second window. Both windows share the same delivery point, last 1 hour, and have zero grid or storage losses. In the baseline schedule, all 10 jobs run in the first window alongside a fixed 5 MWh load in the second window. Shifting q MWh yields demands of (10 − q) MWh and (5 + q) MWh in the two windows, still completing 10 jobs and consuming 15 MWh in total. These service-equivalence and lossless assumptions are explicit boundary conditions of the example.
claims.scope: Author-constructed hypothetical task, equal-service premise, and two-window electricity quantities
caveats: All numerical parameters are author-constructed and represent neither ERCOT observations nor inputs from the German dispatch study.

claims.text: Each window has two available supply resources dispatched in merit order—lower cost first until capacity is exhausted, then higher cost. In the first window, the cheaper source supplies up to 5 MW at 100 kg CO₂/MWh and the costlier source supplies up to 10 MW at 700 kg CO₂/MWh. In the second window, capacities are 10 MW and 5 MW at emission rates of 300 and 600 kg CO₂/MWh, respectively. Maximum energy in each window equals power capacity multiplied by its 1-hour duration. The two windows are independent, omit startup, ramping, and storage constraints, and compare direct CO₂ only.
claims.scope: Fixed supply capacities, merit order, and operating emission rates in the two-window example
caveats: Unit power is multiplied by one hour to obtain energy in this example; results cannot be extrapolated to other durations.

claims.text: At the start of shifting, each MWh removed from the first window avoids output from the 700 kg CO₂/MWh resource, while each MWh added to the second window calls on the 300 kg CO₂/MWh resource, giving a local net rate of −400 kg CO₂/MWh shifted. Shifting 5 MWh changes emissions by −3,500 kg in the first window and +1,500 kg in the second, for a complete net difference of −2,000 kg CO₂ relative to the baseline schedule.
claims.scope: Baseline local rates and complete shift difference before hitting the first binding capacity constraint

claims.text: Increasing the shift to 10 MWh remains feasible, but the active supply conditions change: once the first window's high-emission resource is fully backed down, further reductions cut the 100 kg/MWh source, and once the second window's cheaper source reaches capacity, extra load calls on the 600 kg/MWh source. Total emissions rise from 5,500 kg CO₂ in the baseline to 6,000 kg CO₂ under the 10 MWh shift—a net increase of +500 kg CO₂—whereas extrapolating the initial net rate would falsely predict −4,000 kg CO₂. At a 9 MWh shift, the two windows' changes cancel exactly at 5,500 kg CO₂, showing that crossing the initial 5 MWh validity bound does not immediately reverse the sign to a net increase.
claims.scope: Active-set change, exact emission difference, and failure of initial-rate extrapolation across a capacity boundary

claims.text: Now change only the second window's costlier resource from 600 to 300 kg CO₂/MWh so that it matches the cheaper resource. Once the first resource in the second window hits its capacity limit, the second resource must still supply the extra load, yet the incremental emission rate per added MWh stays unchanged. A change in binding constraints or active generators therefore does not automatically invalidate a numerical emission rate. Even so, only the second window's factor stays constant; the first window still switches rates, so the full shift cannot follow the initial net rate throughout, and shifting 10 MWh in this control case yields a complete net difference of −1,000 kg CO₂.
claims.scope: Matching emission rates across replacement units can preserve one endpoint's factor across an active-set change

claims.text: A single load-shifting proposal therefore involves three distinct, separately testable judgments. Observed low-response time groups can suggest candidate schedules; once both endpoints and system constraints are specified, a fixed dispatch model can compare the two complete schedules; and claiming that the modeled difference will occur in reality still requires evidence matching the node, timing, and intervention. The stylized example isolates how shift magnitude alters modeled results. In the Cambium discussion that follows, weighting hourly rates by load changes produces a coefficient-based response estimate; whether that weighted sum equals the joint dispatch change of a specified finite plan still requires verification rather than being guaranteed by the summation formula.
claims.scope: Conditional synthesis across observational screening, finite dispatch-model differences, and real-world intervention evidence

claims.text: When a demand change persists long enough to influence power-plant investments or retirements, the fixed generating fleet assumed above can itself evolve. Distinguishing short-run from long-run estimates begins by checking whether the model allows capital stock to adjust: a figure labeled with a future year may still represent a short-run dispatch estimate on a fixed future fleet. We next examine a scenario framework that allows both operations and generating capacity to respond.
claims.scope: Which assets future demand changes can alter; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: Cambium 2024 links capacity expansion to hourly dispatch through a chain of coupled models. The Regional Energy Deployment System (ReEDS) models generation and transmission buildout, retirements, and planning constraints; the Distributed Generation Market Demand (dGen) model projects behind-the-meter photovoltaics; the Probabilistic Resource Adequacy Suite (PRAS) checks resource adequacy; and PLEXOS solves hourly unit commitment and dispatch given the resulting capacity. Here "2024" denotes the release vintage, while the annual table values examined below come from the 2025 simulation year.
claims.scope: Which assets future demand changes can alter; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: Cambium's long-run marginal emission rate (LRMER) is derived from two full model runs: a baseline and a perturbed case with higher end-use demand. End-use electricity demand across the modeled footprint is scaled upward while preserving its load shape—by 1% in the 2025 simulation year and by 5% in all other solved years. Both ReEDS and PLEXOS are re-solved so that operations and capacity can co-evolve before changes are attributed to regions and hours. LRMER therefore estimates the response to a finite national-scale perturbation rather than a local partial derivative from adding 1 kWh in a single state and hour.
claims.scope: Which assets future demand changes can alter; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: Generation differences between the two runs must then be allocated to consuming regions. Cambium allocates technology-level generation increases using network flows under a complete-mixing assumption at each node and nets out corresponding decreases. Whenever a technology's net change in an hour is negative, the calculation excludes it from that hour's marginal mix on the ground that the decrease may stem from investment or operational shifts driven by other hours rather than the hour's incremental load. Because those removed decreases are not reassigned to the hours that actually induced them, the published metric embeds this attribution choice.
claims.scope: Which assets future demand changes can alter; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: Two resource types require tracing back to earlier hours. Storage discharge originates from prior charging and incurs round-trip efficiency losses; Cambium approximates its source using the receiving region's monthly mix of non-storage, non-energy-limited generation, adjusted for round-trip efficiency. Energy-limited resources such as hydropower may either add net energy or shift existing energy across hours; the method inspects each technology's monthly net change to separate incremental energy from shifted generation and approximates replacement generation for the shifted portion from the source region's monthly mix without applying storage losses. After physical attribution, state clean-energy portfolio requirements are enforced through an averaged emission-attribute transfer—without tracking individual certificates—before finally converting rates to end-use electricity.
claims.scope: Which assets future demand changes can alter; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: The published annual electricity table can be checked for approximate balance. Taking the MidCase scenario, ERCOT region, and 2025 simulation year from the same release package, regional generation of 438,493,630.0 MWh plus 412,059.4 MWh of imports minus 1,208,316.6 MWh of exports equals 437,697,372.8 MWh. Subtracting the tabulated busbar load of 437,697,380 MWh leaves a residual of −7.2 MWh. Small as it is, that residual should be retained: published numbers verify only approximate balance and cannot reconstruct internal solver precision.
claims.scope: Which assets future demand changes can alter; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: Whereas the previous check reconstructed busbar load from generation and trade, we can also sum the components of busbar demand from the same row: 425,158,500.0 MWh of busbar electricity serving end-use load, 4,366,699.0 MWh of interregional transmission losses, 8,168,517.0 MWh of battery charging, and 3,672.7 MWh of pumped-hydro charging. Those four terms exceed the tabulated busbar load by 8.7 MWh, leaving a second small residual whose cause cannot be resolved from displayed values alone. End-use consumption also includes behind-the-meter photovoltaics—electricity generated and consumed on the customer's side of the meter—and the tabulated busbar load serving end use scales that behind-the-meter output by distribution losses into a busbar-equivalent quantity. Because behind-the-meter generation never traverses the distribution grid, its busbar-equivalent component cannot be counted as metered grid purchases, nor can total busbar load—which includes transmission losses and storage charging—be treated as delivered end-use electricity.
claims.scope: Which assets future demand changes can alter; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: Moving from the busbar to end users brings in the distribution layer. In the same row, end-use electricity equals 409,876,104.3 MWh, which is 15,282,395.7 MWh—about 3.5945%—below the busbar electricity serving end use. That difference represents distribution-level losses, distinct from the separately reported interregional transmission losses. Cambium also distinguishes average from marginal distribution losses, applying average losses to average and long-run metrics and marginal losses to short-run metrics. Factors already published per end-use MWh must not be multiplied a second time by a delivery-loss adjustment.
claims.scope: Which assets future demand changes can alter; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: Delivery boundaries also shift direct CO₂ emission rates. In this scenario row, the generation-weighted average is 235.2 kg CO₂/MWh generated, whereas the consumption-based end-use average is 249.7 kg CO₂/MWh end use. Bridging those two numbers involves imports and exports, storage sourcing and attribution rules, and distribution-loss conversion, so dividing the generation rate by a single delivery ratio cannot reconstruct the end-use rate—nor can either scenario figure be treated as an updated version of the historical eGRID regional rate for the same system.
claims.scope: Which assets future demand changes can alter; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: Expanding the inventory boundary adds precombustion processes and converts methane (CH₄) and nitrous oxide (N₂O) into carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂e). Under this broader scope in the same MidCase row, the end-use average emission rate is 307.5 kg CO₂e/MWh, the short-run marginal emission rate is 757.8 kg CO₂e/MWh, and the long-run marginal emission rate is 547.3 kg CO₂e/MWh. All three share the same end-use denominator: the first attributes scenario supply emissions to consumption, the second estimates operational change with fixed capital, and the third allows capacity to adjust with load. Selection depends on the analytical question; relative magnitude alone never proves one model more accurate than another.
claims.scope: Which assets future demand changes can alter; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: The greenhouse-gas aggregation behind that long-run metric can be checked term by term. In the Cambium 2024 workbook for ERCOT, 2025, and MidCase LRMER, the direct combustion components per end-use MWh are 409.1 kg CO₂, 15.5 g CH₄, and 1.99 g N₂O. Converting grams to kilograms and weighting by the workbook's 100-year global warming potentials (GWP)—1 for CO₂, 29.8 for CH₄, and 273 for N₂O—gives 410.10517 kg CO₂e. Applying the same weights to the precombustion components of 41.5 kg CO₂, 3,209.1 g CH₄, and 0.19 g N₂O yields 137.18305 kg CO₂e.
claims.scope: Which assets future demand changes can alter; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: Summing the combustion and precombustion equivalents gives 547.28822 kg CO₂e/MWh, matching the published 547.3 kg CO₂e/MWh to one decimal place. This arithmetic verifies how individual gas masses combine into the reported metric without re-solving the capacity or dispatch models. Although fuel extraction, processing, transport, and fugitive emissions enter the precombustion term, plant construction, non-combustion operation and maintenance, and decommissioning remain outside the boundary, so this CO₂e figure cannot be shortened to a complete life cycle impact of electricity.
claims.scope: Which assets future demand changes can alter; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions
caveats: The numerical check does not propagate underlying statistical, parameter, or model-structure uncertainty; displayed decimals reflect tabulated calculation values rather than equivalent measurement or predictive precision.

claims.text: Altering future scenario assumptions changes the modeled rate substantially. Switching to the low renewable-energy cost and high natural-gas price scenario (LowRECost_HighNGPrice) for the same region and 2025 simulation year raises the long-run marginal metric to 638.4 kg CO₂e/MWh—91.1 kg CO₂e/MWh above MidCase. Because that scenario varies technology costs, performance, and fuel assumptions together, the gap cannot be attributed to a single price parameter. Such comparisons contrast conditional futures rather than proving which pathway the real grid will follow.
claims.scope: Which assets future demand changes can alter; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: Applying an annual rate to a specific intervention first requires knowing when load changes. If hour h experiences a demand change Δqₕ under a response rate mₕ, the total emission change is ΣmₕΔqₕ; dividing by total net energy change to obtain a unit rate is valid only when net energy change is non-zero, whereas load shifting can alter emissions while leaving net electricity use unchanged. Gagnon and Cole compare distinct load shapes within the same modeling family precisely to examine this temporal weighting. Because Cambium uses standard time, hour-beginning timestamps, and a 2012 weather and calendar year, its timestamps must be converted before aligning with EIA's 2023 hour-ending records, and annual averages must be checked for their aggregation rules.
claims.scope: Which assets future demand changes can alter; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: A further discrepancy can be checked directly from the annual loss formula. The Cambium 2024 documentation denotes annual variable distribution losses as L_v,annual and annual busbar load as Q_annual, printing the coefficient as L_v,annual / Q_annual² multiplied by each hour's Qₕ². Summing across all hours recovers the prescribed annual loss only if the denominator is ΣQₕ², whereas Q_annual² equals (ΣQₕ)² and generally differs. The cited Borenstein and Bushnell working paper uses the sum of squared hourly loads. Inspecting the printed equation identifies this mismatch, though which expression the generating code actually executed remains to be verified, and published annual tables are not altered on that basis.
claims.scope: Which assets future demand changes can alter; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: Connecting an electricity change to a full life cycle inventory requires linking responding technologies to their background supply chains. Vandepaer and colleagues (2019) construct long-term marginal mixes from growing, unconstrained technologies in prospective scenarios and link them into ecoinvent background processes, voltage markets, and impact assessment methods. Because U.S. regional shares are disaggregated from national projections, fine geographic labels do not prove locally measured responses. This mix-construction rule also differs from Cambium's joint capacity-and-dispatch re-optimization, so comparing the two requires aligning background database versions, delivery boundaries, and impact assessment methods.
claims.scope: Connecting electricity responses back to life cycle questions; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: Different claims require different validation evidence. Re-running native code verifies numerical pathways under fixed inputs; comparing against a full re-solve of the same model tests internal approximations; and testing against empirical data requires aligning space and time while showing that the observed proxy represents the target response. For example, Koebrich and colleagues' 2023 preprint evaluated earlier Cambium hourly signals against 2021 observational proxies, which does not yet test the long-run capital counterfactual of the 2024 release examined here; moreover, the authors' affiliation with WattTime—which provides competing emission signals—should be disclosed alongside the evaluation design.
claims.scope: Connecting electricity responses back to life cycle questions; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: Tracing an electricity intervention to emissions follows a clear sequence: specify how demand changes across hours to deliver the same final service; identify which network segments carry the power and how generation and trade are attributed; and determine whether existing unit dispatch or generating capacity responds. Assessing broader environmental impacts then requires specifying how each emitted substance and resource flow enters impact characterization. The cases above illuminate separate links in that chain; the next chapter turns to recycling, examining what services recovered paper fiber, heat, and electricity deliver and which supply streams they displace.
claims.scope: Connecting electricity responses back to life cycle questions; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: Once a corrugated paperboard box has been used, it may be collected, repulped, and manufactured into another paper product. Analysis begins by tracking where the recovered material goes and what the recycling mill actually produces. With that physical trail established, a second question asks which product carries the burdens of waste treatment and reprocessing. Evaluating an additional batch of collected paper raises a third question: whether recycling, virgin production, or incineration elsewhere changes in response. Although these three steps can be linked into a single assessment, each requires its own evidence.
claims.scope: Distinguishing physical flows, burden attribution, and market response in recycling chains

claims.text: In 2005, the Danish Environmental Protection Agency (Danish EPA) published a study by Frees et al. drawing on 2001 paper-flow statistics and mill data to compare scenarios with changing recycling volumes and to evaluate what happens when an additional 1 kg of collected paper is sent to recycling rather than incineration. The report separates fractions including newspapers and magazines, corrugated board, and mixed paper. Focusing on corrugated board, this chapter first traces how much paper domestic recycling mills receive and what grades they produce, then examines which virgin paper grades and energy supplies the report uses as references.
claims.scope: Historical question and selected paper fraction in Danish EPA Environmental Project No. 1057

claims.text: The unit of comparison in this study is 1 kg of collected wastepaper. The model follows that kilogram through recycling or incineration and the corresponding supply adjustments, without modeling corrugated board forming, box fabrication, or the use phase, and without testing how much cargo a box can safely carry. Linking recycled mill output to displaced virgin paper therefore requires separate evidence on paper grades and mechanical strength. In what follows, "quality conversion" refers to material quality and functional performance; equal tonnage establishes only equal mass.
claims.scope: Distinction between waste-treatment service and packaging service

claims.text: Tracking the annual flow from collection to reprocessing starts with the report's baseline ledger. Denmark's annual corrugated board consumption and collection potential is modeled at 346 thousand metric tons (kt), of which 275 kt are collected and the remaining 71 kt are assumed to be incinerated. Because the 275 kt collected total includes 66 kt of production and converting scrap, it cannot be described entirely as post-consumer boxes. Adding 22 kt of imports and subtracting 114 kt of exports leaves 183 kt of feedstock entering domestic recycling mills. Even within this single annual material account adopted by the study, the locations of use, collection, and reprocessing do not coincide.
claims.scope: Annual baseline commercial paper-flow ledger in Environmental Project No. 1057

claims.text: The study's annual ledger can also be checked against the upstream statistics it cites. In the 2003 Danish recovered-paper statistics report, the corrugated packaging flowchart sums empty packaging supply and net imports of filled packaging to reach 346,371 metric tons of total supply. Combining domestic mill consumption, net exports of recovered paper, and stock changes yields 274,780 metric tons collected, yet the collection-rate calculation box in the same figure prints 274,704 metric tons. At the displayed precision, both figures give a collection rate of roughly 79.3%. Moreover, the import and mill-consumption values in that statistical diagram differ from the figures later adopted in the 2005 model. Although these arithmetic relationships can be checked, the reasons for the discrepancies remain undocumented, so the two tables cannot be spliced into a single exact inventory even though both refer to the same year.
claims.scope: Upstream statistical reconstruction and cross-report discrepancies

claims.text: With domestic mill input established, the next step is to calculate output per kilogram of feedstock. The 183 kt of annual input correspond to 144 kt of linerboard and fluting plus 23 kt of another paperboard grade. Dividing both outputs by the 183 kt domestic total yields approximately 0.786885 and 0.125683 kg of finished product per kg of feedstock; the report's unit scenario uses the rounded values 0.787 and 0.126, summing to 0.913 kg. The remaining 0.087 kg is simply an output-mass gap at this reporting level. Because it does not reveal how much of that difference consists of fibers, fillers, contaminants, or moisture, it cannot be labeled a "fiber loss rate."
claims.scope: Product output ratios versus fiber component mass balance

claims.text: A closer look at mill operations explains why that residual mass cannot be equated with fiber loss. As described in the report, the SCA mill takes both recovered corrugated board and other mixed paper as feedstock, sending them through pulping, staged contaminant removal, sheet forming, pressing, starch application, and drying. Landfilled residues such as glass and stones and incinerated residues are recorded separately. Although primary feedstock and finished board share the same reported dry-matter fraction, additives and residues have no closed fiber-component balance. Mill-wide ratios therefore characterize this blended operation, but they do not establish the pulping yield of pure corrugated board or the number of cycles a fiber has actually undergone.
claims.scope: Mill-wide mass ratios versus fiber-specific mass balance
caveats: The Skjern mill branch has its own process configuration and residue destinations and cannot be merged directly with SCA mill residues.

claims.text: Holding the physical destination of a material constant isolates the effect of changing allocation rules. In 1997, Ekvall and Tillman illustrated a material serving three successive products: V₁ denotes the burden of virgin material production for the first product, R₁ the recycling burden from the first product to the second, R₂ the recycling burden from the second to the third, and W₃ the final waste-management burden after the third use. The shared pool to be partitioned is V₁ + R₁ + R₂ + W₃, while each product's own manufacturing and use stages are accounted for separately. This three-use sequence is a stylized chain constructed by the authors; the Danish statistics do not track a single batch of fibers through it.
claims.scope: Idealized three-product cascade from Ekvall and Tillman (1997), not an observed Danish fiber chain

claims.text: Under one rule presented in the 1997 paper, the product that initially extracts the material also bears the burden of its eventual disposal, giving L₁ = V₁ + W₃, L₂ = R₁, and L₃ = R₂. Final waste treatment still physically occurs after the third product is discarded; only its accounting burden is assigned back to the first product. Summing the three product shares confirms that each of the four physical activities is counted exactly once.
claims.scope: Fixed-process burden partitioning under Equations (10)–(12) of Ekvall and Tillman (1997)

claims.text: A different rationale leads to different shares. In his 1999 doctoral thesis synthesis, Ekvall describes a rule in which virgin production and final disposal are split equally between the first and last products, while each recycling step is split equally between the two products across that handoff. Applied to the three-product chain, this yields L₁ = (V₁ + W₃ + R₁)/2, L₂ = (R₁ + R₂)/2, and L₃ = (V₁ + W₃ + R₂)/2. Summing the three shares again reproduces the full process ledger. Even when the physical material flows and delivered services remain identical, the two rules assign different burdens to each product; choosing between them requires a justification for assigning responsibility to the respective products.
claims.scope: Three-product shares derived from the 1999 textual 50/50 rule

claims.text: Checking the sum also uncovers a printing error in the original literature. Equations (16)–(18) in the 1997 article originally contained minus signs; a formal 1998 erratum corrected the three numerators to V₁ + W₃, R₁ + R₂, and V₁ + W₃, respectively, but left the final term of Equation (16) printed as R₂/2. Summing the three equations strictly as amended by the erratum exceeds the complete process ledger by (R₂ − R₁)/2—a discrepancy that vanishes only if the two recycling steps happen to carry identical burdens. The adjacent-handoff expressions in the preceding paragraph follow Ekvall's 1999 textual statement, and the original printed equations and published erratum must be preserved as distinct records.
claims.scope: Algebraic discrepancy between the published 1998 erratum and a remaining typographical subscript

claims.text: Encountering a "50/50" label also requires checking what quantity the factor of one-half multiplies. Ekvall's 1999 thesis separately describes a two-product method attributed to Vigon et al. that splits the net consequences relative to a no-recycling baseline, incorporating avoided virgin production and avoided waste treatment, whereas the rule above partitions actual process burdens. Even though both rules apply the same 50/50 split, dividing different underlying quantities produces results with different meanings.
claims.scope: Different quantities partitioned under identically named 50/50 rules

claims.text: In its schematic cascade linking newsprint, molded egg trays, and corrugated board, the Danish EPA report represents each handoff through avoided production. Where the first system subtracts credit D₁, the second system inherits that same D₁ as its reference burden, and D₂ is handled symmetrically. When the accounts of all products in the chain are summed, each matched D term cancels out. If the upstream product claims an avoided-production credit while the downstream product also claims the same benefit, the ledger no longer conforms to the diagram. The figure illustrates an accounting rule; verifying the actual life history of a specific batch of fibers still requires separate physical tracking.
claims.scope: Conceptual reference-handoff scheme in Figure 3.2 of the Danish EPA report

claims.text: Calculating avoided production requires specifying what is being displaced. For recycled linerboard and fluting, the Danish EPA report constructs a pure virgin process specifically for system expansion, while the other paperboard grade is matched against an integrated paperboard process using sulfate (kraft) pulp and chemi-thermomechanical pulp (CTMP). As the authors note, several commercial grades already incorporate recycled fibers in practice, so the pure virgin reference does not represent an observed standalone mill. The model treats additional recycling as displacing virgin paper on the premise that recoverable wastepaper is supply-constrained and demand for recycled products is not limiting. A mill's receipt of wastepaper confirms physical routing, but confirming actual displacement requires market evidence.
claims.scope: Identity and assumptions of modeled virgin reference processes

claims.text: Once the reference grades are defined, an annual increase in collection can be translated into modeled virgin-paper displacement. In the scenario holding imports and exports constant, domestic mills receive an additional 18,000 metric tons of wastepaper diverted from incineration, and the report calculates 16,000 metric tons of additional finished board. Applying the report's equal-strength assumption—that 1.25 metric tons of recycled linerboard and fluting are needed to match 1 metric ton of the corresponding virgin grade—yields 12,800 metric tons of avoided virgin production. The first figure measures extra mill output; the second measures the modeled reduction in virgin production after strength adjustment. Changing the conversion ratio to 1:1 alters only the modeled virgin displacement, leaving the mill's physical output unchanged.
claims.scope: Quality conversion in the report's annual increased-collection scenario

claims.text: Returning to 1 kg of feedstock connects each product grade to its own reference. In the domestic corrugated-board recycling row, Table 3.1 of the Danish report specifies modeled substitution ratios of 0.8:1 for linerboard and fluting and 1:1 for the other paperboard grade. Multiplying the unit yields gives 0.6296 kg of modeled virgin linerboard and fluting from 0.787 kg of recycled output, and 0.126 kg of reference virgin paperboard from 0.126 kg of recycled output, where 0.8 is the reciprocal of the 1.25 factor above. These two products are derived from the disclosed grade yields and substitution ratios rather than printed as a complete activity vector in the original table. The two reference grades cannot be collapsed into a single generic "virgin fiber," nor does the annual scenario's simplified conversion of total output prove that all grades share the same ratio.
claims.scope: Derived relationship between grade-specific substitution ratios in Table 3.1 and product yields in Table 4.6

claims.text: The 1.25 factor originates from a 1994 personal industry communication cited by the Danish report. Alongside it, the report notes earlier industry statements ranging from claims of no performance difference to views—in a different recycled-content comparison—that heavier board is required. Because paper grades, furnishes, and box designs are not aligned across those statements, they do not form a single statistical basis. The 1.25 ratio represents the performance conversion chosen for the report's model, whereas fibers screened out during reprocessing are process losses that must be accounted for first in the material balance.
claims.scope: Provenance and scope of the historical 1.25 strength ratio

claims.text: The 0.833 figure found in waste-management pulp literature likewise requires provenance checking. In their 2009 solid-waste study, Rigamonti et al. assumed one initial use plus five recycling loops, spreading the burden of virgin pulp across six uses so that 1 kg of secondary pulp corresponds to roughly 0.833 kg of net virgin-pulp substitution, with thermomechanical pulp (TMP) as the tabulated comparator. That number follows from an assumed cycle count and burden-allocation rule; answering how much pulp wastepaper yields, or whether Danish board grades substitute at equal strength, requires separate evidence.
claims.scope: Model origin of the 0.833 pulp substitution factor in Rigamonti et al. (2009)
caveats: The five-recycle assumption cites Comieco (2008), with no identifiable primary empirical data supporting its generality across paper grades; original standard requirements are not inferred from later guideline citations.

claims.text: A 2018 follow-up paper recommends first identifying the process step where substitution can occur and then listing collection and reprocessing losses incurred before that point separately. Placing substitution at the pulp-production stage in the paper example makes it possible to verify that the same loss is not deducted twice. That paper reuses the 2009 calculation without adding an independent mechanical-performance test. Linking a pulp-stage burden factor to a finished-board strength conversion therefore requires establishing how the two are related rather than simply multiplying the coefficients together.
claims.scope: Point of substitution and prohibition against multiplying distinct factors
caveats: The 2009 and 2018 studies share two authors (Rigamonti and Grosso), and the later article directly reuses the earlier model; independence is limited by this shared methodology and data lineage.

claims.text: Determining how many times paper can actually be repulped requires physical testing. In a 2020 German study, Kreplin and Putz repeatedly repulped and reformed sheets from individual grades as well as a blend of kraftliner, testliner, and recycled fluting. How many cycles the fibers in the commercial recycled grades had already undergone was unknown, and the blend tests adjusted pulping energy and process-water recirculation to limit filler loss. What the study tracks, therefore, is how this specific furnish changes in properties under a defined experimental protocol.
claims.scope: Materials and experimental design of the independent German multi-recycling study

claims.text: Across 25 laboratory cycles on the blended furnish, the Concora Medium Test (CMT) flat-crush force declined from 146 N in the first cycle to 138 N in the 25th, while other grades followed different trajectories. Pilot-scale trials ran for 16 cycles, with added calcium carbonate raising filler content in the final cycle, and the authors explicitly caution against comparing the laboratory and pilot series directly. The trials also omitted industrial unit operations such as pressure screening and cleaning, and sample removal in each cycle gradually depleted the remaining stock, setting a practical limit on the run. These results refute the notion that five cycles represent a universal physical ceiling, yet they do not justify assuming infinite recyclability, constant industrial yields, or equal cargo protection from boxes of equal mass.
claims.scope: Experimental sheet-forming cycles, laboratory metrics, and boundaries for industrial extrapolation
caveats: The Concora Medium Test (CMT) measures the flat-crush force of laboratory-fluted strips and cannot substitute for protective-performance testing of finished corrugated boxes.

claims.text: Judging whether two paper grades can substitute for each other begins by specifying the intended function. Sheet tensile strength, fluted-medium flat-crush resistance, and box compression strength are measured by different tests, and transport conditions may also bring humidity and cargo protection into play. Holding one indicator constant does not prevent filler content, basis weight, or other properties from changing. A conversion ratio is warranted only when end use, structural design, material dosage, and performance all align. Mill yield, performance-based substitution ratios, and multi-cycle burden factors answer three distinct questions—and even when technical substitution is feasible, whether external production actually declines still depends on the market.
claims.scope: Conditions for moving from material testing to functional conversion

claims.text: Diverting a batch of wastepaper from incineration also alters the heat and electricity exported by the incinerator. The Danish report's incineration scenario takes paper or board at 92% dry matter, yielding 12.53 MJ/kg of combined heat and electricity before distribution losses—roughly one-quarter electricity and three-quarters heat. Deducting separate transmission and distribution losses leaves 2.81925 MJ of delivered electricity and 7.518 MJ of delivered heat, rounded in the report to 2.82 MJ and 7.52 MJ. Although both are expressed in megajoules (MJ), electricity and heat deliver two distinct services.
claims.scope: Delivered heat and electricity from the same incineration branch

claims.text: The report's earlier aggregate approximation illustrates the pitfall of summing energy outputs. Dividing the 10.34 MJ of combined delivered heat and electricity by a 77% efficiency credited roughly 13.4 MJ of avoided natural gas input. The problem is that the reference natural-gas combined heat and power (CHP) plant delivers heat and electricity in a 1:1 ratio, whereas wastepaper incineration delivers them in a very different proportion. Matching total megajoules does not match the two services individually: scaling back the reference CHP plant to match the heat output removes more electricity than the incinerator supplies, requiring an explicit source to make up the shortfall.
claims.scope: Equal total energy does not ensure equivalence of joint energy services

claims.text: Balancing heat and electricity separately changes the net energy credit substantially. Matching the incinerator's displayed 7.52 MJ of delivered heat reduces output from the 1:1 reference CHP plant by 7.52 MJ of heat and 7.52 MJ of electricity—15.04 MJ in total—which, at 78% delivered efficiency, avoids roughly 19.28 MJ of natural gas. Because the incinerator supplies only 2.82 MJ of electricity, the remaining 4.7 MJ shortfall must be met by marginal power-only generation at 50% efficiency, consuming 9.4 MJ of natural gas. Subtracting the two leaves a net avoided natural gas input of roughly 9.88 MJ. That compensating electricity generation is required to hold both energy services constant and cannot be omitted while retaining the larger avoided-fuel credit.
claims.scope: Joint heat-and-electricity service reconstruction from displayed report values

claims.text: Both calculations start from the same energy exports at the incinerator: the earlier method equates total energy, whereas the compensated method equates heat and electricity individually. Because the reference CHP efficiency also shifts from 77% to 78%, the drop from 13.4 to 9.88 MJ cannot be attributed solely to compensating electricity generation. Furthermore, the report applies this compensation only in the 100% incineration unit scenario, so interpreting the annual scenarios requires checking which energy-accounting rule each scenario actually used.
claims.scope: Interpretation of the rule change and its actual scope in the original model

claims.text: For heat-only recovery, the report defines a separate branch in which the incinerator generates no electricity and exports the entire 12.53 MJ/kg of pre-loss energy as heat, departing from the one-quarter-electricity, three-quarters-heat split above. Two accounting methods are reported side by side: using reference data allocated by exergy gives 3.4 MJ/kg of avoided natural gas, whereas switching to system expansion with compensating electricity gives 6.04 MJ/kg. Both figures come directly from the report. However, a conditional recalculation that applies the previous section's 1:1 CHP ratio, delivered efficiency, and compensating power efficiency after deducting 20% heat-distribution losses from the 12.53 MJ yields roughly 5.65 MJ/kg rather than 6.04 MJ/kg. Because the report does not disclose the intermediate parameters needed to explain that gap—nor the specific factors used in its exergy allocation—the two methods can be compared accurately as reported, but neither figure can be presented as independently reproduced from published parameters.
claims.scope: Reported exergy-allocation versus system-expansion comparison and unclosed recalculation

claims.text: These checks verify one local relationship within the energy module, not the entire model. The original study relies on the Danish UMIP (EDIP) database, last updated in 2002; its appendices tabulate selected process and reference contributions, but omit the full activity matrix, item-by-item background dataset identities, and unrounded precision. Likewise, the "process primary energy" reported in the appendices is not identical to the "avoided natural gas input" discussed in the methods chapter and cannot be compared without specifying the conversion. Re-running the full model or judging whether its findings still hold today therefore requires additional primary evidence.
claims.scope: Boundary between partial relation checks and full model reproduction

claims.text: External responses also unfold in the wastepaper market itself. Collecting more paper locally may induce other mills to use more recycled fiber, or price adjustments may depress collection elsewhere. In a 1999 schematic, Ekvall connects a focal system's purchases and sales of secondary material to supply and demand in external systems. Where public policy directly constrains recycling rates, marginal responses must be reassessed against the governing rules. Knowing that local collection increased does not by itself determine how global flows change.
claims.scope: External collection and external demand as targets of market response

claims.text: In a 2000 Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE) paper on paper-bag distribution, Ekvall worked through a quantitative example assuming that the wider market is much larger than the focal change and that prices mediate collection rates. Under the paper's default elasticities, roughly 44% of an additional unit of secondary supply translates into higher external demand, while roughly 56% displaces collection from other sources. Only after that market split is estimated does the analysis ask how much virgin fiber the additional recycled fiber displaces. The first step estimates who adjusts purchasing or collection, and the second tests whether material applications match; neither quantity can be read from Danish mill yields.
claims.scope: Source-reported market shares in the SAE paper-bag example, not Danish observations
caveats: The source inspected is an author-posted excerpt of the SAE paper rather than the full text of the companion Resources, Conservation and Recycling article from the same year; the 44/56 split is a model output obtained under default parameters for that example.

claims.text: The default elasticities in that SAE paper were drawn from a U.S. municipal solid-waste policy model. Ekvall cited an earlier Resources for the Future working paper by Palmer, Sigman, and Walls for its secondary-material supply and demand elasticities, while noting that collection schemes, regulations, geography, and time horizons can all shift those elasticities. Explaining market responses in Denmark or Sweden during that period therefore still requires local empirical data.
claims.scope: Original geographic and policy-model provenance of the default market elasticities

claims.text: Mill-level input demand complicates the substitution assumption further. In a short-run Swedish mill demand model, Lundmark and Söderholm found that recovered paper and wood pulp behave as substitutes for some grades but can act as complements in others, such as newsprint. Because the model holds output and capital fixed and does not estimate full supply-side collection responses, it cannot directly quantify how much wood-pulp production changes when an extra metric ton of wastepaper is collected. It does, however, provide an empirical basis to question which processes actually increase or reduce virgin pulp use.
claims.scope: Short-run mill input-demand relationships as a check on universal substitution assumptions
caveats: The source inspected is an excerpt from the version included in Lundmark's 2002 doctoral thesis rather than a page-by-page verification of the subsequent journal article, and it does not establish a global response.

claims.text: The external critical review of the Danish EPA report already flagged this issue, observing that raising collection in Denmark could reduce collection in other countries and that crediting all recovered fiber with displacing virgin wood favors recycling scenarios. At the same time, the review explicitly noted that it had neither verified the fitness of input data for the stated purpose nor audited calculations line by line. That critique pinpoints a pivotal assumption behind virgin substitution, while confirming individual inputs and results still requires returning to the underlying data, models, and calculations.
claims.scope: Actual coverage and reservations of the original Danish critical review

claims.text: Even after material, heat, and electricity outputs are balanced against the same services and references, changing the reporting object can still alter the ranking: if a full-system route comparison favors material recycling over energy recovery, will the footprint allocated to the original product point in the same direction? As shown earlier, a single material chain can be partitioned into different burden shares. Extending that question to a comparison of two end-of-life routes means holding the underlying activities and references fixed and asking how much of the net benefit is credited to the life cycle of the product generating the waste. A smaller credit to that product does not shrink the net benefit of the full system; how other systems inherit the remainder depends on the governing allocation rules.
claims.scope: Distinct objects of product-level footprint shares versus fixed-activity route comparisons

claims.text: The Circular Footprint Formula (CFF) supplies a concrete accounting rule for this handoff. In Version 6.3 of the 2018 Product Environmental Footprint Category Rules (PEFCR) Guidance, the net end-of-life material-recycling term is multiplied by 1 − A and the net energy-recovery term by 1 − B before entering the current product's footprint. Each net term combines treatment burdens with the subtracted reference production; A partitions burdens and credits between the supplier and user of recycled material, while B governs what share of the net energy-recovery term is assigned to the current product. Because A and B act on different interfaces, their values need not match. Recycling rates, reprocessing losses, quality conversion, and residual disposal each enter the full formula separately, so A or B alone cannot determine the environmental outcome of a waste stream.
claims.scope: End-of-life burden-sharing structure in Equation 18 of the 2018 PEFCR Guidance v6.3

claims.text: In 2021, Ekvall et al. used a hypothetical waste-polymer comparison to show how the two accounting perspectives can produce opposite rankings. In their Figure 3, the full-system net benefit of material recycling exceeds that of energy recovery, yet with A = 0.5, a secondary-to-virgin quality ratio of 0.9, and B = 0, the material-recycling credit assigned to the original product ends up smaller than its energy-recovery credit. Because the two calculations in that figure also treat the quality of displaced virgin material differently, the illustration is not a pure ceteris paribus test of changing allocation factors alone; it demonstrates a possible accounting outcome rather than empirical waste-plastic data or a recalculation of Danish corrugated board. In the same article, a baseline model of Swedish bio-based low-density polyethylene (LDPE) using average heat and electricity references shows lower climate impacts for mechanical recycling under both accounting approaches, confirming that changing allocation shares does not automatically reverse the ranking.
claims.scope: Contrasting rankings between the hypothetical Figure 3 and the Swedish baseline model in Ekvall et al. (2021)

claims.text: Reading that figure also requires tracking where the quality ratio enters the equation. The formula subtracts quality-adjusted virgin production from the recycling-process burden before applying the allocation factor; the 0.9 ratio scales only the displaced virgin production and does not trim the recycling-process burden itself by 10%. Consequently, the product's allocated credit cannot simply be described as 45% of the full-system net benefit. Because the figure's full-substitution reference and product-footprint reference apply different quality treatments, the ranking reversal cannot be attributed purely to changing allocation shares. Isolating the allocation effect requires harmonizing material performance and displaced quantities across both sides before comparing shares.
claims.scope: Placement of the quality ratio in the CFF and control conditions for isolating allocation effects

claims.text: That isolation can be stated algebraically. Let M and H denote the positive net benefits of material recycling and energy recovery, respectively, for the same waste batch under a single impact indicator, after accounting for treatment quantities, treatment burdens, and material, heat, and electricity references normalized to identical services, with all other terms equal or canceling out. While the full-system ledger favors material recycling whenever M > H, the original product's allocated shares can still satisfy (1 − A)M < (1 − B)H and thus favor energy recovery. Nothing here reduces the full system's M; only the share credited to the original product changes, and multiplying both net benefits by the same positive factor would preserve the ranking. This derivation holds only under the stated control conditions and cannot be applied unexamined when quality treatments diverge, residual disposal terms do not cancel, or net benefits are non-positive.
claims.scope: Author-derived algebraic control under positive same-indicator net benefits and matched residual terms

claims.text: Nor does this allow practitioners to tune B freely to obtain a desired footprint ranking. In the 2022 English corrigendum of the European Union Product Environmental Footprint (PEF) method (Commission Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279), both weighting parameters remain in place: B defaults to 0 unless an applicable specification in Annex II Part C provides another justified value, and any upstream use of a non-zero B must prevent double counting in the energy-using system. Because the 2018 PEFCR Guidance already set B = 0 as the default alongside a formal review pathway for alternative values, later academic proposals cannot be described as the first permission for a non-zero B. The value of roughly 0.6 proposed for Sweden in Ekvall et al. (2021) reflects a local benefit structure; it does not automatically become an applicable product parameter, nor does it demonstrate that physical energy output declined by 60%.
claims.scope: Separate attribution of the 2018 review path, the 2022 PEF default and exception, and the 2021 Swedish proposal

claims.text: When physical activities themselves change, the comparison shifts altogether. Ekvall et al. (2021) also examined capacity-constrained incineration, where sending additional domestic waste to a full plant displaces imported waste that must then be treated elsewhere. Under a constraint on total energy input to the incinerator, the extra domestic waste crowds out an energy-equivalent quantity of imported waste; if heat and electricity recovery and delivery conditions remain unchanged, domestic energy exports stay nearly constant, and the net change shifts to the treatment and associated energy supply of the displaced waste. In that situation, those displaced activities must be tracked explicitly rather than counting the full crowding-out consequences while still crediting the added domestic waste with full avoided local energy production. Adjusting B changes only the reported share of a net term; altering these external activities changes the net term itself.
claims.scope: Modeled displacement under energy-input capacity constraints versus allocation-factor adjustments

claims.text: Returning to that 1 kg of collected paper brings the evidence chain together: first verify which reprocessing system it enters and which grades emerge, then specify where treatment and recycling burdens change hands. Explaining the advantage of recycling over incineration further requires accounting item by item for the heat, electricity, and paper products delivered by each route and identifying which external processes respond. Mill output ratios belong to the material ledger, service-conditioned conversion belongs to functional performance testing, and changes in production or collection belong to market analysis. Only by linking all three can an assessment establish the conditions under which recycling is advantageous—and identify which relationships must be rechecked when paper grades, end uses, or markets change.
claims.scope: Synthesizing the evidence chain for recycling arguments from the historical case

claims.text: Comparing material designs through a product footprint and comparing two waste-management actions through a full-system assessment therefore address distinct questions that must be kept clear. The former reports what a product carries under a specified accounting rule; the latter measures how physical activities differ under equivalent services and a chosen counterfactual. When their rankings diverge, the discrepancy points to differences in allocation, references, or modeled activities—not proof that one calculation is erroneous, that recycling is generally unfavorable, or that modeled benefits actually occurred on the ground. Judging which action is preferable still requires returning to comparable full-system activities and their supporting evidence, whereas reporting a product share requires stating explicitly which burdens and credits were assigned to it. For the 1 kg of paper examined here, at least two questions must be asked separately: what share is assigned to the product under the specified rule, and how do the two complete routes differ when delivering the same paper, heat, and electricity services? Missing evidence on paper grades, energy references, or market responses must bound the corresponding claims rather than be papered over by adjusting allocation factors. Having traced how joint production, market responses, power systems, and material recycling chains reshape activities and inventory flows, Part IV turns to midpoints and endpoints to follow the environmental pathways through which those emissions and resource extractions translate into distinct impact indicators.
claims.scope: Conditional judgment separating product-share reporting from full-system waste-action comparisons
